subtopic: YARMOUTH-BAR HARBOR-INAUGURATION OP SERVICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to make a statement concerning the inauguration of the ferry service between Yarmouth, Nova Scotia, and Bar Harbor, Maine, by the vessel Bluenose.
It had been expected that this vessel would be delivered on July 17 and the service would begin at the end of July. Unfortunately, after the trial runs last week it was found that some of the bearings of the gears had overheated and that four of them will have to be renewed. Though the shipyard is working overtime on the job, it is expected that renewal of these bearings will delay the delivery of the vessel by about 14 days and make it necessary to postpone for a corresponding time the inauguration of the proposed service.

Then the motion goes on to explain why it is a matter of immediate and urgent public concern at this time.
Standing order 31, when it speaks of urgency, means urgency of debate. It seems to me that this matter is one that should be dealt with in supply while the estimates of the Department of Trade and Commerce are being dealt with. Furthermore it refers to negotiations now taking place and it speaks about a reported price of $19 million, $16 million of which is to be guaranteed by the Canadian government in respect of bank loans to be made for payment of the wheat. As I recall it a question was asked Friday and the reply was given by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) that this matter is still pending. The information given by the Prime Minister Friday was to the effect that the negotiations in respect of this matter were not completely terminated. Therefore the matter referred to in the motion could not be a definite one. I have Hansard here for Friday, July 1, 1955, and I find that at page 5557 the Prime Minister is reported as saying:
I know that the negotiations have been proceeding, Mr. Speaker, in what we consider to be a satisfactory manner, but I have not been informed that they have been concluded. The negotiations did deal with a large quantity of wheat, and did deal with the insurance by the Export Credits Insurance Corporation of a substantial portion of the price to be paid within twelve months, I understand.
Apparently that is the situation with respect to this transaction as of last Friday.

It is laid down that where the right of appeal is refused then, in order to test the attitude of the house towards it, there is an appeal from the refusal to grant a direct appeal.
At page 747 of Beauchesne's third edition we find that on February 19, 1932, at a time when the Hon. George Black was Speaker, this is the notation:
The Speaker's refusal to permit an appeal from his decision that it is not urgent to adjourn the house for the purpose of discussing an urgent matter of public importance being appealed from was confirmed by the house.
Mr. Ralston, from his place in the house, asked leave under Standing Order 31, to move the
Wheat-Negotiations with Poland adjournment of the house for the purpose of discussing a definite matter of urgent public importance, and stated the subject to be:
"The recent dismissal of between 200 and 300 officers and men of the Royal Canadian Air Force without regard to their families, their overseas service or their period of enlistment or service, and the embarrassing situation which may arise if they were forced by the necessity for employment to accept service with another nation."
Mr. Speaker ruled that the statement was not in order and that the matter was not one of urgent public importance and moreover that there was no appeal from his decision.
Mr. Ralston appealed from the Speaker's refusal to permit an appeal from his decision.
And the question being put by Mr. Speaker: Shall the ruling of the Chair be sustained; it was decided in the affirmative.
On the basis of that ruling, Mr. Speaker, I ask that there be an appeal from your first decision that there is no right of appeal in this connection.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: REPORTED SALE OF 10 MILLION BUSHELS TO POLAND    MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
I probably should have asked the Leader of the Opposition when he heard me say that I refused an appeal. He assumed that I was refusing the appeal. However, I welcome the recitation of the ruling which is found at page 747 of Beauchesne's third edition. I will merely point out to the Leader of the Opposition, just so we do not detract from the practice which has been established, that the rules as we have them today under standing order 31 which gives responsibility to the Speaker for deciding whether a question is of urgent public importance were included in our rules by the revision committee of 1927. I would ask him to reconsider his stand at this moment in view of the fact that the first time there was an appeal from the Speaker's ruling was during Mr. Speaker Black's speakership. Mr. Ralston wanted to appeal. Mr. Bennett shared the view of the Speaker that when he decides a point of practice there is no appeal. That is standing order 12. If he decides a point of order, there is an appeal; but if it is his responsibility to use his own judgment, as it is his duty under standing order 31, with respect to a matter which is a matter of opinion, Mr. Bennett and Mr. Speaker Black were of opinion that there was no appeal. Mr. Ralston appealed from the decision of the Speaker that there was no appeal.
Now, there were several occasions when standing order 31 was moved. And the Leader of the Opposition will find that only on one other occasion, when Mr. Speaker Fauteux was Speaker, an appeal in similar circumstances to a decision of the Speaker that there was no appeal was granted. On all other occasions the house has always accepted the decision made by the Speaker, and also has always accepted the view that in those circumstances there was no appeal from the Speaker's ruling.

Now, at this moment, what the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) is asking is that we revert back to 1946, once, and then to 1932-that is, of having a third appeal of the decision of the Speaker that there should be no appeal. It seems to me that our practice has been so firmly established that the Leader of the Opposition should not pursue, I think, the point of appealing the Speaker's ruling that there should be no appeal, because that point has been so firmly established.
I would like to make this appeal to the Leader of the Opposition: The rules do not belong to the Speaker; they belong to the whole house. When a practice has been established, I think that members, especially those who have responsibility for giving tone to the whole debate, should help to maintain this practice-unless on this bright day of the 5th of July, 1955, it is felt that what has been done in the last 15 or 20 years has been a very wrong practice, and that it needs to be righted.
Now, in the circumstances, if that is the position of the Leader of the Opposition, I will certainly be pleased to give him the right to appeal because, although, mind you, I will say I could tell the Leader of the Opposition he has no right to appeal in the circumstances,
I am not going to take that view. I am simply going to appeal to him again to consider what has been the practice back throughout ' these years-if only on two occasions, and I shall give the references to the Leader of the Opposition after I have seen my notes later this day-so in the circumstances I would simply ask him to reconsider the decision that he has proposed.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: REPORTED SALE OF 10 MILLION BUSHELS TO POLAND    MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31

Mr. Speaker, since you have invited me to reconsider I would point out that you have said, yourself, that on other occasions the house has accepted the decision.
I had indicated that, with respect, I do not feel the reasons for refusing the debate are consistent with our practice. Therefore when Your Honour speaks about giving tone to the debate I have no intention of taking up what that might be regarded as implying. But I do say this, very emphatically, that I believe the tone of the debate will be well maintained if the opportunity is offered to members to express their opinions. And my opinion has already been indicated very firmly, that the way to avoid commitments that, in honour, we would be called upon to carry out, is to debate this now, let the house have the facts and let members express their opinions, so that the government may have the advantage of the opinions of the members in regard to something that many of us think should not go forward.


Having regard to that statement-that it is consistent with proper tone in debate-I think that members should have an opportunity to express themselves on this. Therefore I do ask for the opportunity to have members of the house express their opinions in a definite way.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: REPORTED SALE OF 10 MILLION BUSHELS TO POLAND    MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
Perhaps the Leader of the Opposition misunderstood me. When I used the word "tone" I did not intend to refer to the debate. I was referring to the maintaining of a practice with respect to the rules. The Leader of the Opposition is under a misapprehension. The decision as to whether the motion should be debated is one thing; and once the decision has been made, he is not appealing from that decision, because I take the view, as my predecessors have, that once I have made that decision there is no appeal under standing order 31. He appeals my ruling; that is, my expression of the practice that there is no appeal. Now, having done all I can in order to persuade the Leader of the Opposition that an appeal in this case should not be made, if he feels there should be, I shall put the question to the house.
Those who are in favour of sustaining the Speaker's ruling will please say yea.

maintopic: REPORTED SALE OF 10 MILLION BUSHELS TO POLAND    MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31

speechtext: Nay.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons

speechtext:
The question is on the matter of an appeal from the Speaker's ruling that there was no appeal on his decision to refuse to accept a motion to adjourn the house under standing order 31 when pursuant to paragraph 3 of standing order 31 he thinks it is not in order and of urgent public importance. I based my ruling on the practice which has obtained in respect to these matters over the years, and I wish to refer hon. members to a ruling by Mr. Speaker Casgrain on March 10, 1939, in which the Speaker indicated that there was no appeal. He said:
This is not a question of order which has been raised, and there is no appeal from the decision of the Speaker. Under standing order 31, Mr. Speaker is simply asked to state whether he thinks the matter should be submitted to the house. There is no appeal. There is no point of order there.
Discussion followed, but the Speaker then called the orders of the day and the incident was closed.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: REPORTED SALE OF 10 MILLION BUSHELS TO POLAND    MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: I declare the Speaker's decision sustained. So that there be no recurrence of this situation, may I refer the house to what was the situation prior to 1927. I hold in my hands now a ruling of Mr. Speaker Rhodes which appears in Beauchesne and which is of April 2, 1919, in which he defined urgency of debate:

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: REPORTED SALE OF 10 MILLION BUSHELS TO POLAND    MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
There is one point mentioned by the hon. member to which I would reply, and more especially for the benefit of proper decorum in the house on the matter of urgency. Urgency, within the meaning of the rule, is not a question whether the matter proposed to be discussed is of urgent importance-it may be of infinitely urgent importance to those affected-the question is whether it is urgent within the meaning of rule 39; in other words, whether it is a matter of that urgency which would cause harm to the public interest if the ordinary opportunities provided by the rules of the house were not able to permit the subject to be brought on early enough. I submit upon that point that the mere circumstance that yesterday afternoon the hon. member had an opportunity and that he will have an opportunity again the first time on going into supply is a sufficient answer.
In 1927 they amended the rule. Rule 39, section 4, at the time was amended and the paragraph which was amended reads as follows:
He then hands a written statement of the matter proposed to be discussed to the Speaker, who, if he thinks it in order and of urgent public importance, reads it out and asks whether the member has the leave of the house-
And so on. In the explanation provided when this amendment was proposed the committee did say this:
This section provides that the mover of an adjournment motion for the purpose of discussing a definite matter of urgent public importance hands a written statement to the Speaker, who, if he thinks it in order, reads it out and asks whether leave of the house is granted. There is doubt as to whether the Speaker must only decide as to the form of the motion. The rule as amended will be clear.
In other words, from that moment on the Speaker does not decide only as to form but decides also whether he thinks that it is in order and of urgent public importance, and urgency is urgency of debate. It would seem rather unsound that there should be an appeal

speechtext: The house resumed, from Monday, July 4, consideration of the motion of Mr. Howe, Port Arthur (for Mr. St. Laurent) for the second reading of Bill No. 256, to amend the Defence Production Act, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Brooks.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext:
Last night in the course of my remarks, Mr. Speaker, I had asked the government and the Minister of Defence Production (Mr. Howe) to consider further our suggestion that instead of proceeding with this bill as it is now drawn they should withdraw it and bring forward a bill which would have the effect of dividing the Defence Production Act into two parts, one part being established on a permanent basis and the other part containing those powers which it has previously been agreed by the minister and the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) should not be made permanent and which would be continued then on the basis that they would expire unless renewed from time to time by parliament. I pointed out that that proposal is contained in the amendment moved by the hon. member for Royal (Mr. Brooks) and was repeated by the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low). I hope the government will see fit to accept our suggestion. I imagine that if they want to do it on their own initiative instead of referring it to the banking and commerce committee to have that committee do it, there would be no reason why that should not be done. What we are concerned with is having the suggestion we put forward adopted in principle; the method might be left to be worked out as seems best under the circumstances.
I then went on to discuss what had been done in the United Kingdom and the United States under two comparable acts. I showed that the extraordinary powers given in those acts-to the appropriate minister in the United Kingdom and the president in the United States-are not permanent but require to be renewed from time to time by their legislatures; otherwise they expire. I discussed the United Kingdom act in some detail, to show that there they preserve the supremacy of parliament in the manner indicated without any damaging effect on their defence effort or their defence production. I suggest that if that can be done in the United Kingdom, there is no reason whatever why the same thing cannot be done here, which is what we are asking.
I do not believe I have, in the time at my disposal, any opportunity to refer in detail to the United States act. I am quite sure I shall have an opportunity to discuss that in detail on another occasion in the course of this debate. I might say that it is quite obvious that unless the government does accept the very sensible compromise we have suggested-

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext:
We are not impressed by threats, I will tell you that. We are not a bit impressed.

speechtext: You have driven the minister out of the house.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext:
-in this debate has been
the rather unusual strategy used by the government in carrying on the debate, or perhaps one should more properly say the lack of strategy. If any strategy on their part is involved, it would seem to me that it is a sort of scorched earth tactic in the
5690	HOUSE OF
Defence Production Act hope that after weeks of pursuit the opposition will become exhausted as a result of the rigours of this climate and for other reasons, and give up and go home.
But I feel sincerely, Mr. Speaker, that this is a very important topic and that we should not be turned aside from our prime objective of safeguarding the rights of parliament. It is true that on a few occasions, if one were to carry on the simile, a lone horseman has appeared in view. As soon as he has been seen, he has immediately galloped off in all directions. Some of these horsemen have never been seen again, and we are not quite sure whether they have been rewarded with special leave for bravery or whether they have been banished to the Liberal equivalent of Siberia, whatever that may be, for allowing themselves to be seen. From time to time, too, one of their field marshals, decorated with his well earned honours in previous campaigns, has appeared on one flank and then on the other in the hope we will be distracted to one side or the other and go off in pursuit of him on the assumption, I presume, that it would be reasonable to suppose that where there is a field marshal there is an army. So far as we can determine, there is no army, and we are not going to be turned aside from our objectives in that way.
One hon. member who took part in this debate briefly, from the government side of the house, was the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Philpott). He took very strong objection to a statement I had made in the course of the debate on a previous occasion. I am sorry that other commitments prevented my being in the house when the hon. member spoke, because had I been here I could have put him straight. I believe it was not his intention to misinterpret what I said. Referring to a speech I had made earlier the hon. member said on that occasion:
The results speak for themselves. When an hon. member gets up in this house and likens the request of the Minister of Defence Production, for legislation to enable him to carry on his job, to the request of Adolf Hitler for the concession of complete totalitarian powers in Germany, that, stated in the mildest and most parliamentary terms, is hitting so far below the belt that it should not be condoned by any hon. member in this house.
I could have told the hon. member then that it was not my intention on any occasion to make any odious or other comparison between the Minister of Defence Production (Mr. Howe) or any other member in the house and Adolf Hitler or any other well known totalitarian. My sole purpose was to show that in the beginning our parliamentary systems are whittled away, by degrees, in what appear first to be harmless
[Mr. MacLean.l

ways. That was the point I was trying to make on that occasion. And I suggest if hon. members would care to read what I did say they will be forced to arrive at the same conclusion.
I was trying to point out that it is when we first change from the course he have been following for centuries, that of parliamentary supremacy, to some other course, that we may unwittingly very shortly run into danger. Innocent procedures, or procedures that are made to look innocent, are the thin edge of the wedge, and can well lead to danger, and even to complete loss of our parliamentary rights.
If I could use another simile, when one is a navigator-and this simile is often used- it is when he changes his course that he makes a mistake. He may be in perfectly safe waters, but if he changes his direction he may soon find himself on the shoals or, even worse, may wind up in a sort of stagnant Sargasso sea of bureaucracy.
I would point out again that it is vitally important that we safeguard most jealously the rights, privileges, and responsibilities of this House of Commons. Had it been my intention to make a comparison between an hon. member and Adolf Hitler-and that was not my intention-the comparison would have been between the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) and Adolf Hitler, because this is the Prime Minister's bill. He introduced it to the house. It is his responsibility and rightly so, because he is the Prime Minister and it is his duty to accept responsibility for decisions made by his cabinet.
If he were to seek the advice of members of his cabinet

and I think he should-then I say, with all due respect, that perhaps the minister directly concerned should be the one who should have the least to say in the matter. Because, after all, it affects him more than it does any other member of the cabinet. The administration of his department is, of course, his responsibility. Whether it is administered properly or efficiently is something for which he should answer when his estimates are before the house.
In any case, Mr. Speaker, this is not a matter of personalities. By its very nature it would be impossible for it to be a matter of personalities. It is a matter of principle for this simple reason, if for no other: All of us are mortal. Our days are numbered. But if this bill were approved in its present form, the powers would go on forever. It is not a case of deciding whether or not the present minister is a suitable person to have these extraordinary powers. Rather, it is a case of

deciding whether all ministers of defence production in Canada, from now on, should have these extraordinary powers. When one is considering that, he must also realize that ministers of defence production of the future may not even be members of the house at the present time, or may not even be born yet.
In a recent speech the Minister of Defence Production assured us that he was on the side of the angels. All of us would like to feel that we were on the side of the angels; but I think we would be the least capable of judging whether we are or not. It has been said that proud man, clothed in a little brief authority, plays such tricks before high heaven as make the angels weep. So we should, I think, be humble; we should be very careful before making the assertion that we are on the side of the angels-unless we mean by that that our intentions are good.
I cast no aspersions whatever on the minister's good intentions; I know they are of the best. I just doubt whether he is the best judge of whether or not he is on the side of the angels.
If we can look at this matter in an impersonal way, or remove it from the personality of the present Minister of Defence Production, we might visualize some future ministers in that department having these extraordinary powers for an indefinite length of time. While I do not know, I would hazard the guess that if the Minister of Defence Production were called upon to make from the membership of the House of Commons a list of those who could be trusted with these powers indefinitely, I believe the list would be a short one. I doubt for instance if it would include the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green), or the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) or the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) or the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore) or, for that matter, the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Philpott), the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Croll) or even the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris).
I would be happier with the situation if the Prime Minister had taken a more active part in this debate. I was pleased to see him rise in his place yesterday and make a brief speech. After all, it is his responsibility to see whether there will be a Department of Defence Production or not, and under what powers it will operate, if it does exist. It is his responsibility to appeal to this house, or, to use a slang expression, to sell to this house the necessity for such a department with such powers. After all, the Minister of Defence Production, in his capacity of Minister of Defence Production, is a creature of this
Defence Production Act house, and when that is being discussed it would be only reasonable to expect the attitude of the creature to its creator to be courteous when the matter of his continued existence is under discussion.
I was pleased to see the minister rise in his place yesterday and consider the possibility of ways of reaching common ground. It is true to say that all members of this house have good intentions and are determined that Canada shall have the best possible defence. In addition to that, we in this part of the house feel we should safeguard at all costs our hard-won parliamentary institution. Many suggestions have been made as to a possible compromise. It has already been suggested that there is no necessity to pass this bill during this session. After all, the present act does not expire until a year from now, and surely, if this debate has served no other useful purpose, it has convinced the employees of the Department of Defence Production that this house feels the department should continue on a permanent basis. Practically everyone is agreed on that point.
No real explanation has been given as to why the suggestion to drop this bill at the present time is not acceptable. Another suggestion that has been made is to put a time limit on the bill itself, or to separate it into two parts, and put a time limit on the section which deals with these objectionable powers, powers which would be objectionable at least on a permanent basis.
I myself have already suggested that this act might be repealed completely. That would have the effect of ending the suspension of the Defence Supplies Act, and an act which would not include powers of a special nature could be introduced to set up the Department of Defence Production on the same basis as any other department of government. The present Defence Production Act suspends the Defence Supplies Act, and it will remain suspended indefinitely if this bill passes in its present form.
The leader of the Social Credit party, the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low), suggested a compromise yesterday which I think merits serious consideration. Although I give the Prime Minister credit for seeming to want to seek common ground yesterday, I will be bold enough to say that the compromise he suggested is not an acceptable one. If I can illustrate it in simple terms, he said this: If I were to lend some money that I had in trust to a borrower, that borrower would give me the right in three years to ask him for it, but he would retain the right to say whether he would pay it back or not. That is not good enough. What we in this group demand, as it were, is to have a promissory
5692	HOUSE OF
Defence Production Act note incorporated in this bill saying that the powers we are turning over to the minister will be returned to us at some early date in the future, and that then parliament can again decide whether it wants to extend the loan or not. We do not want to lose custody of our possession. I am therefore forced to say, Mr. Speaker, that if one were to lend money on the basis that he can ask the borrower at some future date if he wants to pay it back or not, an agreement of that sort, in the minds of the people, would not be worth a tinker's dam.
When speaking recently, the Minister of Defence Production told us of the possible horrors of atomic warfare. I for one sympathize with the minister in regard to the great load of responsibility he carries in providing suitable material for the defence of this country. These are rapidly changing times, and we must face them with faith, strength and confidence. Although I sympathize with the minister in his apparent shuddering at the possibilities of the future, I must nevertheless admit that it might be an indication he is no longer flexible enough to adjust himself to these rapidly changing times. We are in a position now where we must face the future with imagination, with faith in ourselves and in our institutions and, perhaps most important of all, in the belief that in right there is some might. I think that ideas and ideals are perhaps worth more in the armoury of democracy than bombs, even atomic bombs.
Of course, this idea of dreading the future and the extraordinary scientific advances that have come about in recent times is understandable. It is not a new thing. After all, human beings tend to be afraid of something that is new, unknown and strange. In that regard I should like to make one very brief quotation from a man called Robert Barrett, written in 1598, with regard to some terrible new invention of that date. He had this to say:
Well wishing in my hart (had its bene Gods will) that this infernall fierie engine had never bin found out.
He was speaking then, of course, of the cannon. The situation today is just a projection of that same state of affairs, that progress, greatly accelerated, of course, so that we must adjust to changing conditions so much more rapidly. The minister made reference in his speech to the munitions and supply act and said that there was nothing new in this act that was not in the munitions and supply act. Originally that act had a time limit, but it was amended to cut out the time limit. That is true; but the situation has changed. It was perfectly well understood 

that, if the munitions and supply act was enacted to take care of a temporary situation, a situation that was not going to last indefinitely, namely world war II, it could be only of short duration; but now we find ourselves in an entirely different position. We find ourselves in circumstances which may last as long as we live, as far into the future as we can see and further, and we must be prepared to frame legislation that will be permanently accepted.
The fact that the munitions and supply act was considered by all to be temporary should go unquestioned. If there is any doubt in anyone's mind, I should like to quote from a speech by the Right Hon. William L. Mackenzie King in moving second reading of the bill to establish a department of reconstruction on June 20, 1944. He said:
For example, the Department of Munitions and Supply was set up to carry on an important phase of war work. When the war ends that department will fade out; but, with the preparation for peace and for developing the national economy to further the pursuits of peace, it will be necessary to have some one department that will be specially charged with that all-important work. The Department of Reconstruction will have that particular duty.
It is quite obvious from the statement of the then prime minister that the munitions and supply act was only temporary. It has been said that power tends to corrupt and that absolute power tends to corrupt absolutely. I am not sure that that is the case; it probably is. But I am not going to suggest that power has worked this corruption on the present Minister of Defence Production. However, I say that on some occasions when he takes a very truculent attitude towards what we try to put forward in the most reasonable terms possible, as was so ably done by the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton), with regard to the corresponding legislation in the United States and Great Britain, one wonders if he is not trying to prove the thesis that power corrupts.
In any case, if we as a parliament were to turn over to any minister of the crown, for all time, the responsibility which has been delegated to us on a temporary basis by the people who have elected us, we would be betraying our trust. I think it is unfair to expect our parliamentary institution to commit constitutional hari-kari of that nature, even if the weather is hot. It has also been said that power is a desolating pestilence that pollutes whatever it touches. In the case of the Minister of Defence Production, I think that five years of power has not polluted him. It would be unkind to say that. But we are just trying to make sure that he or any of

his successors will not be exposed to such polluting power for an unnecessary length of time.
It is hard to believe on some occasions in this debate that this is a question of what is the best method to carry on our defence production. Sometimes I cannot help feeling that it is a question of pride, that someone has made a mistake he does not wish to admit. That is not the characteristic of a great man. Of course, it is one of the human frailties, I suppose, to follow the characteristics of animals that have the herd instinct, which was so ably illustrated by the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings (Mr. Nowlan) yesterday when he said that there grows up naturally a herd leader or a king stallion or a bull of the woods, or whatever you want to call him, and that sooner or later there comes a time when he must be deposed and he will be deposed by some younger and abler herd leader. The old herd leader, of course, stands on his pride. He has shown time and time again that he has guts and intestinal fortitude; but he tries to prove the point once too often, and there comes a day when the leader-

The would-be permanent leader of the herd merely proves that he has lots of guts by his entrails being strewn over the area. The herd goes on because it knows change is inevitable. The Minister of Defence Production has directed attention to the necessity for development in many fields of defence: supersonic aircraft, guns, guided missiles and many other things. I agree with him that these things are essential, but I think it also must be admitted that the greatest progress, even in the field of science and development, is made when there is free opportunity for competition and free interchange of ideas. If that requires proof, one could turn to the excellent effort which has been made by the British people as far as defence is concerned, not only since world war II, but prior to world war II. There was no munitions and supply act with great far-reaching powers in existence in the United Kingdom during the early thirties. Yet it was at that time that development contracts were let for the Spitfire, the Lancaster, the Halifax and the Manchester. These were the aircraft which saved Britain in world war II. These developments were made by private enterprise, private companies, working to specifications which had been made by the British government. Of course,
Defence Production Act not all of them were successful. They did not have 100 per cent success. But out of the competition of private firms to meet most nearly the requirements specified, excellent aircraft were developed. The Spitfire and the Hurricane-and chiefly the Hurricane- were responsible for winning for us the battle of Britain; and it was the Lancaster and the Halifax which made possible the night bombing of Germany during world war II. Yet the development contracts for these aircraft were let in the early thirties before there was any immediate sign of world war II.
All that indicates that what is most valuable in the development of new weapons is plenty of lead time; that is, the objectives which one must seek must be set early. In addition to that one must not neglect the affiliated basic resources which make great development possible. Pure research is one of those things. We should remember that in the long run we might defeat our own purpose if we concentrate all our efforts on applied science rather that on pure science. After all, for almost 15 years now, as far as applied science with respect to defence is concerned, we have been relying on discoveries which were made in the field of pure science prior to world war II. It was scientific research done many years ago that made the atom bomb possible, for instance, in world war II. The same is true with regard to guided missiles.
The thing we must be most careful of, Mr. Speaker, is that we do not attempt to set up some all-wise bureaucracy to say what is best and what is the course of endeavour which is likely to prove most rewarding, because there is no possible way of knowing beforehand what that is. One of the classic examples of bureaucrats that were wrong when individuals were right was in the development of the Salk vaccine. The methods pursued in the development of that vaccine were not those which were regarded as being the most likely to succeed by a bureaucratic set-up which was directing research along another line. The same is true with regard to jet aircraft. During the war Frank Whittle persisted in doing research when he was being laughed to scorn by many and when it was said that this research would never reach any useful application. However, it resulted in the jet engine as we know it. Even before world war II was over it provided in the Meteor, the first service jet plane of the R.A.F., a defence against the V-2.
There are other principles too, Mr. Speaker, that we should not lose sight of. I see that my time is almost up and I shall conclude

Defence Production Act quickly. I should like to refer all hon. members to a useful article that has recently been written and published in the Queen's Quarterly by George F. G. Stanley who is, 1 believe, the professor of history at the Royal Military College. This article is entitled "New Ways of War". He reviews carefully the problems which now face the Minister of Defence Production (Mr. Howe) and he ends up by concluding that it is most important that we should not lose sight of the principles for which we stand because if we do that we shall defeat our own purpose in the end.

Mr. Speaker, in considering this amendment moved by the hon. member for Royal, two thoughts come to my mind. The first one is this. Yesterday, when the leader of the Social Credit party made his offer to this house, I was reminded that this offer is substantially the proposal made in our amendment and in the proposals that have been made in every speech that we in this party have made so far in this debate. If nothing else is clear, Mr. Speaker,-if we are in doubt about some of the details of this matter-let us have the record clear in that respect, at least. The debate goes away back to March 10, when it first began.
In the second place,-and this perhaps is a personal reflection and it is the only one of this nature that I intend to make in my remarks today-when the hon. member for Royal was moving his amendment and making his speech, in seeing him across the floor from the Minister of Defence Production I was reminded of the fact that they came here 20 years ago, and my thoughts went back to 1935. They both appeared at Ottawa as a result of the election in 1935 when great


changes took place in Canada. Through the political fortunes of war they sat on opposite sides of the house. It was the fortune of the Minister of Defence Production to be called to the cabinet and to have what we know is a prominent part in government. The hon. member for Royal was destined to become one of the loyal few who have been sitting in opposition for an unheralded and unprecedented 20 years.
I throw out this thought, Mr. Speaker, and I do not mean it in any personal way. When the minister to whom I have referred was sitting in his large office as a cabinet minister directing the affairs of this country during the war, since the war and at other times, the hon. member for Royal was picking up his books in his office and going down the corridors to go into committee meetings and to do his duty in the opposition. I throw out this one thought, Mr. Speaker: Who are we to judge the contributions of these two respective men, or in fact those of any men, as far as war effort is concerned or anything else? I say, Mr. Speaker, that we who are here within the confines of parliament-I am not speaking about the remote comers of Canada-and who know what things are going on do not go back to past achievements. We are judging things today. After all, today is the day we live and tomorrow never comes except when you are taking part in a filibuster.
Having said that, I should like to dwell on the constitutional aspect, if I may use that lordly phrase, and refer to 30 years ago when changes in the functions of our modern government began to become clear. They have been developing since that time, and I suggest that perhaps 30 years ago we saw the first evidence of the change that is so pronounced today. I say that these matters are of concern not only to the lawyers of the country but to every private citizen who can grasp the meaning of our constitution, be it written or unwritten.
Three thoughts come to my mind as to the causes that have changed the function of government. These three thoughts are not necessarily original, but I have tried to connect them with present-day examples that come to mind. First of all, there is the industrialization and urbanization of western society. We have largely become city dwellers necessitating the building up of more and more controls over our conditions of life. There comes to my mind immediately the need for traffic control in our large cities. I think of confusion square outside the parliament buildings and the control that is necessary simply to enable traffic to move around the square. I also have in mind the various

town planning systems that it has been found so necessary to implement in our world today.
Second, there is what might be termed the evolution of a social philosophy. I do not mean for one minute socialism as such. I think it is generally agreed that all parties, the Social Credit party, the C.C.F. party, the Liberal party and the Conservative party, accept in varying degrees the need for some sort of social legislation in the world of today. There is the growth of public utilities so evident in the United States and increasingly so in Canada. It has been necessary to build up various utilities such as telephone systems and other utilities that play a part in our daily lives. This is what I mean by the evolution of a social philosophy. I think of the nationalization that took place in England after the war. All parties agreed that nationalization of the coal industry was necessary. That to my mind is another example of the social change which I am trying to separate from actual socialism.
The third point, one which is of more direct concern and upon which I wish to dwell for some time in relation to the Defence Production Act, is the transformation of our society into a condition where we are almost in a state of emergency-I use that word quali-fledly and will refer to it later-a state of semi-mobilization in which some wartime controls and other compulsory conditions are necessary in this post-war world. The other day there was discussion in the house of the danger of a military junta. To some this seemed absurd and perhaps the occasion was exaggerated, but, after all, according to the words of former prime minister King in 1944, there was a danger, or it seemed so to him at that time, of some sort of military coup d'etat.
I say that this complete change and transformation in our society is going to have a dangerous effect on all our legal concepts. This is a time when it is necessary for the government to make public contracts and to impose health and other legislation on our citizens which formerly was not considered necessary. That is admitted in this debate. It is a day when conservation boards are necessary. We have to be very careful of our national resources. Conventions are necessary to protect our fisheries. Then there are considerations affecting our oil and gas pipe lines and the other necessary requirements for life.
May I close the first part of my introduction by saying that I do not think we are in a state of regimentation as exemplified by
Defence Production Act George Orwell in "1984", but I do admit we are in a very different world from that of 30 to 35 years ago.

speechtext:
I had been saying, Mr. Speaker, that there were three causes for changes in the functions of government in the last 35 years. First, I suggested that the industrialization and urbanization of the west was one cause. Secondly, I mentioned that there had been an evolution in social philosophy. Thirdly, and I was in the midst of dealing with it, there was the transformation of our society itself, and the fact that today there is a definite need for some control. I was stating that while there was regimentation and mobilization necessary in connection with our resources and industry, I felt that it had not reached a critical stage but at least there was no doubt a need for a reconsideration of a lot of rules as a result of this new change.
We have so many of the old cliches used that we wonder if many of them have an application to Canada. There have been the terms, "the new despotism"; "the passing of parliament"; "bureaucracy triumphant"; "the road to serfdom". I ask, Mr. Speaker, do these apply here or are we all right in Canada? Have we nothing to fear from these suggested maladies? The legislature that governs us today perhaps is not susceptible to some of these evils that are inherent in other governments, but I wish to take the time to deal with them. I want to refer to the governments of other countries and the problems they have had with these suggested evils. For the purposes of my remarks here three headings quickly come to mind, and I do not suggest them in any dogmatic way. They will simply help, I believe, with an orderly consideration of the fears I am trying to connect up with this legislation that has been proposed.
First, there is the war power, and where this authority comes from in Canada and in the other countries. Is the constitution written or unwritten? We all agree that the war power of a particular country should be elastic and in these days when we have a post-war period of fears, cold wars and police action, then we want to know where the responsibility and authority of parliament ends and begins. Secondly, I suggest there ought to be a consideration of the executive power. It is the executive power which has increased in practically all the great countries of the world, and this has caused some worry.

Defence Production Act There has been a delegation of power by parliament to the executive in many cases, and in Canada and other countries there has also been the emergence to some extent of the one-party system. This again only increases the executive power.
Thirdly, I refer to the fundamental rights that are involved in any serious consideration of this legislation. I have one definition that I would like to place on the record which will explain in a much clearer fashion the worry that may result from a loss of our fundamental rights. It is Mr. Dicey's definition and is well known to all followers of constitutional law:
First, it means the absolute supremacy of regular law as opposed to the influence of arbitrary power and excludes the existence of arbitrariness, of prerogative or even of wide discretionary authority on the part of the government. It means, second, equality before the law or "the equal subjection of all classes to the ordinary law of the land administered by ordinary law courts". Thirdly, it means that our constitutional law Is not the source but the consequence of "the rights of the individual as defined and enforced by the courts".
Now, having said that there are three divisions of this consideration, I should like to say that the proposed legislation, and particularly the Defence Production Act, which is chapter 62 of the Revised Statutes of Canada, contains many pertinent sections which could be used as examples of these dangers and fears. I will not refer to them directly, but I think I should mention that section 38 would be an example of a section that I feel contains dangerous powers; section 5 would be an example of a section which contains powers that would create a worry about the fundamental rights to which I have referred.
In dealing with the countries and trying to consider these various matters in each case, I think first of all of Canada. I feel, very respectfully, that there is a consideration necessary by private citizens and there is also consideration necessary by lawyers who should be, perhaps, a little better informed on these constitutional matters. The British North America Act does mention various authorities and powers with respect to defence. It is reasonable to suppose that if defence had not been mentioned in any way in the British North America Act there would have been an implied power under the residual clause of section 91 of that act.
Defence is mentioned in one or two instances in the British North America Act. First of all, there is a reference in section 91 to the fact that it shall be lawful for the Queen, by and with the advice and consent of the Senate and House of Commons, to make laws for the peace, order and good government of Canada. This is the catch-all residual phrase, and I would ask that particular

note be taken of this. Then, subsection 7 of section 91 contains a reference to the militia, military and naval service, and defence. This, also, will come into my argument. The other reference, which is not of particular note here, is to section 15 of the British North America Act which reads:
The commander-in-chief of the land and naval militia, and of all naval and military forces, of and in Canada, is hereby declared to continue and be vested in the Queen.
So far as I know, those are the only defence references in the British North America Act.
The two controversial sections that created division are, of course, the residual clauses and subsection 7. It has always been understood that at times when Canada has faced various emergencies, particularly in a time of war, the residual clauses in the British North America Act, those dealing with peace, order and good government, gave the federal government authority to make laws and other legislation for the necessary implementation of procedure for war, or to meet the other dangers that might arise. We have an example of the residual clause being invoked when Canada was not at war when, during the late nineteenth century, there was considerable worry about the drinking of alcoholic beverages in Canada. There was the famous case of Russell v. The Queen which gave the federal government authority to pass the temperance act, which dealt with this serious problem of that time. The federal government was enabled to pass the legislation because it was felt-and this was upheld by the courts-that Canada was in a state of emergency. This decision was upheld, and many other decisions of the privy council, although on one or two occasions Viscount Haldane did limit the use of the word "emergency".
The worry in those countries which have a federal constitution-and I am thinking particularly of the United States and Australia-is not great in this respect, because in. those countries the various powers of the parent governing body are specifically defined in their written constitution. But I do suggest that these two types of worrisome legislation have to be considered again in view of the fact that legislation of this kind is before us today, in which it is asked that continuing or permanent authority be given.
Section 91 (7) of the British North America Act gives specific authority to the federal government to deal with the armed forces, military and naval service and defence, as; well as related subjects. But the general provisions of section 91 do not give authority, except in periods of rare emergency. The use-

of the emergency clause in the British North America Act has to be considered seriously.
We are now in a transitional period. As I have suggested, it is a period of control. I am wondering now whether this piece of legislation should be considered, whether it should be passed under the authority of section 91 (7), or should it come under the residual portion of section 91.
That, Mr. Speaker, creates a very serious problem that could be challenged in the courts at any time. However, we have two examples of emergency legislation being used at times other than times of war. There was the Japanese deportation act, which was upheld by the privy council, and also the leasehold regulations which were invoked where necessary after the war to deal with the housing situation. Both of these were emergency situations. They were not considered actually during wartime but were post-war conditions that no doubt could be connected with the serious prosecution of an all-out defence effort.
Those are the two worries, and I intend to relate them directly with the legislation before us, and to compare them with the situation in other countries. It has been said that, speaking broadly, this legislation could take money out of our pockets, clothes off our backs and our homes from under our feet. I do suggest however that in looking at this matter from the strictly constitutional aspect no very serious consideration has been given to the fact that under this act it is conceivably possible that the Minister of Defence Production (Mr. Howe) could take away our language rights in Canada.
May I offer the thought that if we were in a serious state of emergency, and there developed a shortage of newsprint or printing material which would have to be diverted to the armed forces, the Minister of Defence Production could declare that the duplicate printing of various forms of newspapers or other valuable material would have to be curtailed, and that only a single copy of such printing could be made.
Hon. members may not consider this serious. Nevertheless I do say there is that danger. In leaving that subject, particularly the reference to the Canadian constitution, I would say briefly that this emergency doctrine being applied in the present instance so as to give an excuse for the implementation of this measure, is a matter of more than academic interest for all Canadians, because it is under this particular piece of legislation that all our constitutional safeguards, so necessary in wartime, are included. We have admitted that the provisions are elastic, because the various changes and sudden
Defence Production Act decisions that have to be made are all necessary. I do leave the thought-and I may come back to it again-that under section 91 (7) of the British North America Act there is provision for ordinary and necessary defence legislation, but that when we consider the broad implications of the emergency powers that may be given under the residual part of section 91 there is need for all Canadians to give very serious thought to the matter. I add the further thought that it could definitely be challenged at some later time from a constitutional standpoint.
I have referred to the United States because I believe they have been subjected to this grave worry, and have been in the position of dealing with it-perhaps not too effectively. They dealt with it first of all in the thirties, at the time of the new deal legislation of Franklin Delano Roosevelt. We know that much of that legislation was held ultra vires of the powers of the federal government in the United States. I would refer more particularly however to the steel seizure case, that involving the Youngstown steel company, in which President Truman was involved, at the beginning of the Korean war.
It will be recalled at that time the steel industry was on strike, or about to go on strike, with the result that the supply of steel so necessary to the defence effort was seriously endangered. President Truman stepped in, seized the industry and said that he had inherent powers under the constitution to take that action, because it was necessary for the war effort and the general defence of the United States. There was a good deal of discussion as to his authority and rights in the matter. It will be remembered that a little-known justice by the name of Pine, I believe it was, in one of the minor courts in the land, came out with a remarkable decision which shook the very roots of all belief across the United States, but nevertheless firmly entrenched the justice that does exist in the courts, when he said that there is not a residuum of power in the hands of the president at such times.
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that that same thing could very easily happen in Canada. It has not happened only because we have not had legislation such as this to worry about in the past, that is legislation on a permanent continuing basis. The commander-in-chief of the army, navy and air force in the United States is of course the president; but remember, Mr. Speaker, he does not have authority over the people and industries of that country. His power is definitely limited in that respect. To close the discussion on this legislative problem and the position with
5698	HOUSE OF
Defence Production Act respect to acts similar to this, I should like to quote about four lines from a decision of Mr. Justice Murphy, which referred to the steel case. Mr. Justice Murphy said:
From time immemorial despots have used real or imaginary threats to the public welfare as an excuse for needlessly abrogating human rights. That excuse is no less unworthy of our traditions when used in this day of atomic warfare or at a future time when some other type of warfare may be devised.
I now leave the United States and go to Australia where, as hon. members know, they have a constitution similar to that of the United States. The Australian problem has been dealt with very effectively. They ran into the difficulties which we seem not to have been bothered with, in both the war and peace-war periods. There is a unified government and a definite stand has been taken on these matters, and they have an implied authority in their constitution to deal with all these matters on a residuary basis. The third section of their constitution and the third section of the United States constitution invest a definite judicial power in the federal authority in both cases. There the worry about any further difficulty with legislation such as this and injustices therefrom is definitely considered by their judicial courts, and the great danger of the loss of their fundamental rights of course is not a worry.
There were two cases which I should like to refer to, which definitely bring out certain points and show that Australia has dealt effectively with this problem, which may become a worry to us in Canada. There was the Rola case, which had to do with employment during the war. This case took away judicial powers from the committees. The administrative tribunals and committees felt that they had judicial powers to decide on the basis of the few broad terms that are in these acts, such as matters affecting the rights of employees in government departments. This decision gave back to the courts the right to hear that, and of course took away the authority that the tribunals and committees felt they had. This was not in a time of emergency, and even then the courts upheld the idea that judicial authority and review are paramount.
Then there is the Jehovah's witnesses case, which 1 will not go into. It dealt with the fundamental rights I have mentioned and judicial review of a matter affecting the rights of this religious sect. Their rights were upheld. Therefore, Australia has shown a definite reluctance to give those ministerial tribunals power, as I have indicated.
In France it is a little different. Of course, it is not too serious there because they went through this in 1789. This matter has been


considered in other countries, and was decided in France on a blood basis years ago. Over there the power that is given to their executive is not necessarily constitutional. It is different from the Anglo-American attitude in that respect. The heads of the various executive committees to ensure enactment of laws are given general direction, and they deal with the matter on that basis.
It was interesting to me, Mr. Speaker, to learn that in Germany just the other day when Konrad Adenauer was in the process of getting authority with respect to a volunteers bill in the hope that future plans for West Germany could be effectively formulated, unlimited powers were asked for until March 31, 1956. It caused quite a furore in Germany, and the act that was passed bore little resemblance to the government's own draft. Deputies representing all parties with one exception made it quite clear that they had no intention to write a blank cheque for Chancellor Adenauer or anyone else, so far as Western German rearmament was concerned. In other words, the demand for unlimited powers until March 31, 1956, was completely turned down by the other parties in Western Germany just the other day.
I have dealt with those other countries. Then of course we come to the country which gives us most of our laws anyway, namely, England. They went through this a long while ago. In 1929 Lord Hewart started the ball rolling when he referred to the dangers that were in existence owing to the increase in these various boards and tribunals that were being set up. In that year they formed the now famous committee on ministers' powers. I will not go into that, but there was a thorough investigation of the rights of those tribunals and the powers of the civil servants, and of course the minister's power itself. The reference to the committee was as follows:
To consider the powers exercised by or under the direction of ministers of the crown.
This was in 1929, Mr. Speaker. These people have all been through what we are going through today. The decision was made and the report was published in 1932. An interesting thing comes to mind with respect to that. The committee was set up in England; it was a typical English committee; it was set up in the proper way to do the good work of parliament. It was a bipartisan committee. A Labour government was in power at that time. There were three Conservatives and three Labour members on that committee. How different that is from our own parliament! However, Mr. Speaker, the committee made its report. I must admit that the findings were not startling. They did

say that there was a worry and a danger for the future and unless all the people in England-this may be a little different from here-maintained their sense of social justice, then fears would be well-founded for the future. They also made mention of the fact that the tribunals themselves are legislators, prosecutors and judges of their own acts which they are considering. They also mentioned the fact that the House of Commons was no longer in a position of authority. The scene had changed from the floor of the house to the great departments of state.

No, Mr. Speaker. This is too important a matter, Mr. Speaker, for us to treat it in any hurried fashion. I thought it would be wise if I participated again in this debate. I propose to deal with the subject matter after the fashion of Mr. King, who in 1938, when he was discussing a subject of importance in this house, said, "I shall endeavour in what I say to be as concise and at the same time as comprehensive as possible".
We have had a very interesting debate. Yesterday, I thought, was quite helpful. Quite a number of conciliatory speeches were made. I would commend the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch) and the hon. member for Sim-coe North (Mr. Ferguson) for the efforts they made to speak with the tongue of reasonableness, but I doubt that there was any effect. Of course, later on in the afternoon the Prime Minister entered the chamber, and we welcomed him back. We have missed him in the course of this debate. He gave the stamp of his approval to the debate. We were told that he did not normally participate in discussion unless it were of importance; but apparently this is of importance, as the Prime Minister returned and favoured us with his presence. He did not make a long speech. He did not cover some of the points I had hoped he would cover. He made no explanation of some earlier remarks of his.
Defence Production Act Nevertheless he appeared here and held out to us what was intended to be an olive branch. Others have dealt with this proposal and have shown that the olive branch was not very strong. It was not free from blemish and the fruit on it was very poor and withered.
As I pointed out before, the Prime Minister and the Minister of Defence Production have considerable difficulty in getting together on this subject, and perhaps on other subjects. But the Prime Minister made a proposal to us yesterday about this matter being reviewed at the instance of a private member and at some time in the distant future. The Prime Minister assured us in his remarks, of course, that he was going to be here in the future. This was to allay fear on the part of those who thought he was contemplating moving his residence from the riverside further inland. He was anxious to suggest that the Liberal party was still united and active in the conduct of the business of the country. He and the Minister of Defence Production have difficulty in determining how to deal with matters in the House of Commons. Although the Prime Minister suggests now that reviews should be at the instance of a private member by way of a motion introduced during the course of the next parliament, the Minister of Defence Production told us on June 7, which seems rather a long time ago, and I quote his words from page 4511 of Hansard:
Traditionally this is the way in which legislation can be examined critically, the way in which it can be determined whether or not it meets the needs and conditions of the times.
Just before that he was telling us:
Under our present parliamentary procedures the house has an opportunity to review the responsibilities and functions of each department at least once a year, when the estimates are being considered.
So you see that the Minister of Defence Production says, "Review this when the estimates are up; that is the traditional course of procedure". The Prime Minister says, "No, that is not quite sufficient. A private member may raise the matter on a motion three years hence."
Yesterday the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low) made an able and conciliatory speech and put forward a proposal. It struck some people within this chamber and outside as being new and different. Defence Production Act date. On page 4687 of Hansard I find the following words, and this is the first time I have ever quoted myself in the house.

But this is important, and I am happy to have the close attention of the Minister of Defence Production. He may even burst into applause, and I would quote Dr. Johnson's statement that the applause of a single human being is a matter of great consequence. After I discussed this

matter on June 13, the hon. senior member for Halifax rose and said that I had expressed the greatest confidence in the Minister of Defence Production. For greater certainty, I wish to draw to the attention of the hon. member for Halifax that, because I said that the minister was able, decisive and experienced, it does not follow that I was expressing great confidence in him. Those are all good qualities, but they are not necessarily ones which warrant the placing of great confidence, unless those qualities are used in a satisfactory manner. The minister boasts of his experience. He is a great proponent of experience. Later on-perhaps not this month, but next-I shall examine the experience of which he boasts and show just how much it amounts to. He has been decisive on many occasions. He has made many quick decisions. Some of them have been wrong. He has ability. He has directed that ability sometimes into the wrong channels. I have suggested-

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: Who is this man Churchill that you speak of? Tell me about him. Then you can tell about his views of me.

speechtext: Are you trying to change the subject?

speechtext: Is that relevant?

speechtext: The minister tries to confuse the issue here. speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: And which he does not have.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext:
Outside of the House of Commons the minister may be a delightful character but here on the parliamentary scene I am not sure that I can express the greatest of confidence in him. He gave us two examples of his methods during the course of this debate. Back in March, when we were considering the resolution stage, right after the dinner recess the minister marched into the house and upset the course of proceedings. We were sitting here in our usual diligent fashion waiting to discuss a resolution concerning the Department of National Defence, followed by a resolution concerning fisheries, being the course of business that had been announced the previous evening. We were following the custom of the house as it has usually been followed. When business is announced like that, we know what is ahead. Members were waiting

to take part in that discussion when in walked the minister and said that he wished to go ahead with the resolution on the defence production bill which was third on the list. The hon. member for Vancouver very properly objected. What did the minister say? As reported at page 1962 of Hansard, these are his words, "We are changing the order, that is all".

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: He is the boss.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext:
That type of dictatorial action inspires neither confidence nor respect. Then, for a second example, consider the minister's statement on Thursday, June 28. I promised that I would recite some of his words here just for greater emphasis. As reported at page 5382 of Hansard he said this:
If it had been suggested earlier that it would relieve people's minds ... to put a time limit of five years on the legislation, that might have been considered.
The hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch) dealt with this matter in part yesterday but I should like to elaborate a bit on that statement. What is the record? Right from the very beginning the question of a time limit was raised. On the very first day that the resolution was considered, namely on March 10, the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) raised the question of a time limit and mentioned that the one effective limitation had been removed. On the very next day, namely on March 11, two members on this side of the house mentioned a time limit, namely the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green) and the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell), and they considered a time limit to be of vital importance. On Monday, March 14, three members mentioned the time limit again, namely the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) and the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low). All told, the suggestions ranged from one to four years.
Now the minister says that if someone in March had suggested five years instead of one, two, three or four, that time limit might have been considered. This is a specious argument indeed that inspires neither confidence nor respect. Actually what was going on in March at the resolution stage was a guessing game, and we did not realize it. It was that guessing game-you know it- that children play with their hands behind their back, and with marbles or something like that. They hold them in their hand and you guess how many are in it, and you say three when it should be five. We got caught by that game. My fair-minded friend the hon. member for Greenwood, in his moderate
Defence Production Act and cautious way, suggested one year. My friend the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, who is normally quite an astute parliamentarian, did not even play the game right. He did not mention numbers. He mentioned dates, so he was ruled right out, of course. He did not know what was going on. He spoke of July 1958 or July 1959. The hon. member for Peace River seemed to have a little greater sense of what was going on. He hedged a bit and said one year, two years, three or four; but the proper answer was five. None of us realized that fact in March. I thought that the magic numbers were seven and nine, but apparently there is some magic property with regard to five and, as the minister said, if it had been suggested earlier to put a time limit of five years on the legislation, that might have been considered.
Mr. Speaker, yesterday somebody said that this was parliament at its worst. I think it is the Minister of Defence Production at his worst in advancing arguments of that nature.
We are engaged here in a great historic struggle.

speechtext: Oh, oh.

speechtext: Make no mistake about it, this contest over the Defence Production Act is going to rank as one of the great historic events in the life of the parliament of Canada.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
