speechtext: Number ten.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: Number 18. He has been eating spinach again. There have been other great contests in this house. This one is unique. It represents a trial of strength not just between government and opposition but between parliament and one man. It is obvious now to all who are here-

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: That is absolutely out of order.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: What is the matter with you?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext:
It is obvious to all of us who are here and to the press of the country that the Minister of Defence Production is pitting his strength against not only the opposition but the cabinet and the entire Liberal party. The members of the other house are viewing the scene with interest. Their turn will come next and in their hands will lie a momentous decision. They have it in their power to limit the dictatorial influence of the minister and to reassert the authority of parliament. Nothing like this has happened before in the political history of Canada.

Defence Production Act There have been other strong men but their ways have been different. Macdonald manipulated his fellow men by good cheer and good fellowship, Laurier by sunny ways, Borden by considerate sincerity, Bennett and Meighen by the force of their intellect and logic, and King by devious subterranean methods known only to his biographers; but subtlety is not a characteristic of the Minister of Defence Production. He is as subtle as a dinosaur. What is in his path is brushed aside or trodden underfoot. This experience through which he is passing is unique for him just as it is for parliament. I think it is the first time in his life that he has not been given his own way. For the first time in the 16 years that he has been running the country-

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: Twenty years.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext:
-he has been vigorously opposed. He does not like it and he seems determined to reassert his authority. The minister may win. Of course it will be a Pyrrhic victory. From his knowledge of history I presume that he understands what that means. Our opposition here, protracted and valuable as it is, will eventually be borne down because the rules of the house can be invoked against us with respect to the previous question and closure. Then will follow the vote and we are, of course, outnumbered. All that is required on voting day is a sufficient number of government supporters to stand up and be counted. I can picture voting day, and if I had the skill of an artist I would certainly see it in this way. An Egyptian taskmaster cracking his whip over long lines of slaves, being the Liberal backbenchers, pulling forward a great stone, the Defence Production Act, to be placed on a pyramid which will stand for a thousand years as a monument to Canada's great dictator. I would see the cabinet in serried ranks bending in shameful humility before that taskmaster, and beside the causeway would be strewn the corpses of company managers who had been destroyed. Of course the rollers on which the stone was being dragged forward would be the bruised and mutilated bodies of Her Majesty's loyal opposition. In the background would be a gutted and partially destroyed House of Commons and overhead supersonic planes, guided missiles and the bursting of shells from naval anti-aircraft guns.
This has been an interesting campaign, Mr. Speaker. This is the eleventh day on which the house has given its attention to the Defence Production Act, if you count the resolution stage. In March it was just a skirmish of the forces. We were outwitted,

shall I say. At that time we could have made a long drawn out engagement of the encounter but we were too trusting and we permitted the resolution to pass rather easily. We cannot be sure whether or not we were tricked until the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), who was a party to the arrangement on that occasion, makes an explanation to us. It would be interesting to know his interpretation of the arrangement of March 14.
In June we reached the second reading stage, and then we had a battle on our hands. A surprise attack was launched on us on June 9 when the attention of the house was directed to the Ontario election. We survived that, and between that date and June 28 there were rumours of a compromise, a truce and a peace settlement. But on the 28th of June the minister delivered his ultimatum, and these are his words: "The government must insist that this legislation be passed". There were to be no more games, no more overtures, no more conciliatory speeches, but virtually a declaration that from the opposition side of the house would be required unconditional surrender.
The minister, having come back refreshed from his vacation and having read up on Davy Crockett, is prepared to meet all comers. In the parliamentary struggle he knows he can win eventually by the use of closure. He can control the guerrilla warfare in his rear by counter-measures. The Prime Minister appears to be a captive. I do not know whether he is resting and reading Prescott's "Conquest of Mexico and Peru" and wondering about the troubles of Montezuma. The only remaining obstacles are the upper house and the pressure of public opinion.
The minister knows that the Conservative party, faithful to its belief in the principle of the rule of law, will not resort to violence, and in any case he has supersonic planes and guided missiles. It is important, Mr. Speaker, to know the power of your enemy. Never underestimate your enemy. The minister has said he is working with the angels and he may be right. If I had any means of communicating with the angels I would tell them they would very soon be working for him.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT

speechtext: Is he out communicating with them now?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext:
The reason I say he may be right when he says he is working with the angels is that I have an outside point of view here, and this is my only quotation from

sources outside the house. I will not burden the house with anything other than these four lines, but this is an outside point of view which I thought might be of interest. There is reference to the minister's exploits during the course of the war, and this is what was written:
Howe was expected to build in a few months what, under the best of conditions, should take years. By his own miracle, Howe, who thought nothing of such things, made himself one of the nation's immortals.
The quotation is taken from Bruce Hutchison's book, "The Incredible Canadian". I am sorry he used the adjective "incredible" because he could have made use of it if he had wished to write a biography of this great man. At the time I read it two years ago I was touched with nausea. I feel a little faint right now and I would not mind having a glass of water. Bruce Hutchison, with his great power of description, has given in that sentence a picture of the Minister of Defence Production as he is seen by some people who do not know him as intimately as we do. I note from the dictionary that a miracle is a marvellous event due to some supernatural agency. Here we are worrying about the temporal powers that the minister wants us to give him when he has supernatural powers and is immortal. That means he is going to live forever. Warwick, the king maker, is going to be around for a long long time, and this is bad news for the aspirants to the Liberal throne.
He knows he is going to be here for a long long time. Here are his words as found at page 5382 of Hansard of June 28, and he is speaking, as he likes to do, of his experience and what he has done in the past:
It has been my job for 16 years-
That is the past tense.
-and it is still my job-
That is the present tense.
*-and will be my job

That is the future tense. No wonder, Mr. Speaker, that he broods over this house sometimes silent and inscrutable like the sphinx of Egypt; no wonder that that elusive Mona Lisa smile sometimes flickers across his countenance. When you are immortal you can bide your time and be as patient and imperturbable as Buddha. The minister has told us that he is a collector of exaggerations, and he gave us a few examples. I am also a collector but my collection is composed of the minister's bombastic statements. As collectors I think we should compare notes and perhaps exchange a few. Here are samples
Defence Production Act I have noted from the minister's remarks. Example No. 1, Hansard of the 14th of March, page 1994:
I doubt if there is anyone in the world at present in charge of defence production who has had more experience than I have had-

speechtext: Bravo!

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext:
Example No. 2, Hansard of the 7th of June, page 4512:
In conclusion I may say that I think I can claim to have more experience in defence purchasing than any other man now living.
Example No. 3, Hansard of the 28th of June, page 5378:
Standing here today I am very proud of the fact that in those 16 years I have never undertaken to produce any munitions of war which I have not been able to produce and produce within a reasonable period of time.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext:
I do not think MacNamara's band could do any better.
I have wondered about this debate, Mr. Speaker, and I have wondered about the Minister of Defence Production. He has drawn our attention to one of the causes of insomnia which will be helpful to the medical profession. You get insomnia if you are worrying about $30 million. I would love to get that kind of insomnia. The cure for it is to get another $60 million. It is like taking the hair of the dog that bit you. The minister is causing me insomnia because I have been trying to understand his position.
I realize we have reached the stage here now where there is no sense in trying to appeal to him. What is the sense of trying to make conciliatory speeches at this stage? We did that in March and we did it all through June. Yesterday people coming fresh to the fray tried it again, and where are we? He has taken a position where he declares that the government is determined to push this bill through. He asks us to surrender unconditionally. When you are placed in that position what can you do except resist?
I would prefer, being a man of peace, to discuss these things quietly and reasonably, to debate and argue back and forth, to compromise and reach a conclusion. But we have tried that repeatedly. Everyone on this side who has spoken has tried that without result. Obviously you have to negotiate with the minister from strength, and we know enough about international affairs to realize what that means. We are prepared, I think it is evident, to negotiate from strength. Up to date we have shown that a united force is opposed to the Minister of Defence Production. We are prepared to endure all the agony of an Ottawa summer if need be. I think the minister, in his appreciation of

Defence Production Act the situation, failed to take account of that fact, and failed to take account of the real issue behind this.
Anyone who is viewing this scene might very well ask himself, what is it that has animated the members of Her Majesty's loyal opposition? People who have paid close attention to this debate from March to the present date will see that it is not factious opposition. They know we are just human beings like everyone else. We like relaxation and holidays. We do not like to endure the pressure of this debate and to work through the heat of an Ottawa summer. Surely they see that this is not just a political dodge or a political gamble. I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that you could not get as many people to participate in a debate as have participated in this debate up to the present, under conditions like these and after a lengthy session, and to put up as spirited an opposition as this, unless there was something behind it.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: Whom do you think you are kidding? You don't like publicity?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: If the hon. member wants publicity I suggest he rise and participate in this debate.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: If he has anything worth saying, let him say it.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext:
I was not aware of the reason so many of the members on the opposite side are unable to rise and participate in this debate until I read an editorial in the Winnipeg Free Press not long ago which suggested that they were invertebrates.
What is the issue that divides us? The only thing I may remember in the course of this debate is the minister's statement on June 7, 1955, as recorded at page 4510 of Hansard. He said:
At the resolution stage the Leader of the Opposition implied that in asking for the continuation of the Defence Production Act the government is getting away from traditional methods of parliamentary procedure and parliamentary responsibility, and that there is a denial of the supremacy of parliament and the rule of law. I must admit that I am only a layman in this field-
That is the statement that is going to remain with me when all the rest of this may be forgotten. Yesterday the Prime Minister came into this house and to my shocked surprise he said this, as recorded at pages 5642 and 5643 of Hansard for July 4, 1955. It is unfortunate that Hansard cannot record the emphasis and expression. The words read coldly cannot convey the meaning that was conveyed to this house yesterday. These are the words the Prime Minister used:
On the amendment that was made after quite a large number of speeches had been heard on the terms of this bill and the threat it made to


democracy in this country, there really was nothing that I could add that would have been a contribution to that kind of a debate.
I wish, Mr. Speaker, I could reproduce the impression the Prime Minister conveyed to us when he spoke those words; when he mentioned the threat it made to democracy in this country and "that kind of debate", as if there were something ridiculous and silly about people speaking about a threat to democracy or something ridiculous and silly about our being engaged in a debate of this nature. If the expression and emphasis of the Prime Minister could have been recorded on Hansard it would never be forgotten.
I couple those two things together. The Minister of Defence Production, that great proponent of experience, is a layman with regard to parliamentary procedure and practice after 20 years in this house, and the Prime Minister thinks we have talked enough about the threat to democracy. That is the situation. There has been a gap in the experience of the minister. He does not realize, and I shall point it out to him now because I think I have two or three minutes in which to do it, that in his action in this house he is striking at our heritage and our birthright. He fails to realize that the threat that runs through this measure is a threat to the supremacy of parliament. He has not studied, as we have, the history of parliament.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: The voice of experience.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext:
I can demonstrate it, and I shall when I return to this debate. He has not studied the history of parliament. We know the long struggle from the days of Simon de Montfort until now. We have never severed that connection, our roots have never been cut from that tradition. That is not so with regard to the minister, despite the benefit of the education he may have received. He could not possibly have studied and become conscious of the importance of the long history of parliament as we are conscious of it.
And that is the fundamental issue that confronts us. Until we can impress upon the Minister of Defence Production that he is striking at one of the things we hold dearer than anything else, he will not see the light of reason. We are doing everything in our power to convince him that our cause is the just cause in this instance, and that there can be no doubt about it. That is the proper function of those who are here in parliament. We believe that the basis of our parliamentary system is being affected by

the type of legislation which the Minister of Defence Production is trying to foist upon the House of Commons.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
I should like to say a few words in this debate, although perhaps there is very little that individual members of parliament can add at this time, since nearly all the arguments both pro and con have been trotted out already. Nevertheless it seems to me that a word or two from some private members of parliament on this side of the house might not be amiss. To many members, particularly in the official opposition, who have spoken twice in . the debate, it must be clear that a few of us would like to say just a few words. Accordingly I trust that hon. members will bear with me for a few moments while I make a few brief submissions on the issues, and add one or two personal observations.
I believe most of us are reasonably well informed as to the provisions of the Defence Production Act and all that is involved in being asked to support this bill. It seems quite clear that the official opposition are not really taking issue with the Defence Production Act as such. It has been in force now for a number of years, and we have all had ample opportunity to see how it has worked during those years. I believe I am being fair when I say that the chief issue before the house now is not the provisions of the Defence Production Act, but the extension of those provisions for an indefinite period of time.
Most members of the opposition have gone so far as to compliment-indeed they have not hesitated to compliment-the Minister of Defence Production upon the way he has administered his department over the years. Long ago in the debate the minister must have become tired of the repetition of compliments. I need hardly add that we on this side of the house are proud of him and the wonderful contribution he has made over the years to the public life of Canada. Without a doubt he is acknowledged on all sides of the house as one of the greatest ministers of the crown who has ever served the people of Canada.
May I address my remarks to the chief issue involved, that of the extension of the term of operation of the Defence Production Act. Many hon. members feel that international tension across the world has relaxed, and I would not take issue with that. As a result they feel that the Defence Production Act should not be extended at this time. I believe most of us will agree that the international tension has relaxed; but does this prove that we are not living in
Defence Production Act the most dangerous of times? It is a temporary easing of tension; and does that temporary easing of tension prove that we are not living in a time of emergency?
I believe we are living in very critical times, and I believe most hon. members would agree with that statement. I would say we are living in the face of a world emergency, and that our dear land of Canada is right in the middle of it. Who can tell how long the emergency will last? Who will dare say at this juncture that we should relax, so far as defence production activities are concerned? Will these conditions exist for two more years? Will they exist for three more years, or five? I am sure none of us knows. In the meantime we cannot afford to let the Defence Production Act lapse. No one is asking that; but we cannot afford to let defence production itself lapse, nor to allow the act to come within a year of lapsing. For that reason alone I support the bill.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: What has that to do with the principle?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext:
It has a lot to do
with it. I am giving my speech. You have had plenty of opportunities to give yours. Is the Soviet union cutting its defence production? I just wish to say this; that in a world half in chains and half free we cannot in this part of the world-and a dangerous part of it, at that-afford to relax nor to adopt those idealistic Liberal principles we would like to see exist in this country, in dealing with the present situation.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: Fair-weather principles.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext:
With East Germany behind the iron curtain, with all of eastern Europe under the heel of communism, with Poland broken and its cardinal under arrest without trial, and with Soviet Russia bordering us on the north, is there anyone in the house who will say that the powers contained in the Defence Production Act should be allowed to lapse at this time? In the face of the emergency that faces the free peoples of the world, an emergency that may continue for a number of years-we do not know how long-if for no other reason, I propose that I shall support the bill and vote against the amendment.
There is the further reason that if the Minister of Defence Production is to continue to bear the heavy responsibilities he has borne for many years, if he is to continue to have those responsibilities on his shoulders, he ought to have the power accompanying such responsibilities-power that, so far as I know, he has never abused. This will give

Defence Production Act him the tools with which to do his work. I think we are all agreed as to the necessity for the continuance of the Department of Defence Production, and we are all agreed that there should be some security of tenure for the senior officials in that department. That is what is behind this bill.
We have heard a good deal during the debate about the loss of sovereignty by parliament. However, that argument is not really germane to the issue at all because, as I have said, the official opposition appears to be willing to vote for the bill if a definite date of expiry is inserted. Pictures have been painted during this debate, mostly by members of the official opposition, that would lead persons outside Canada, behind the iron curtain, to believe that in this country we have no liberties at all, that parliament is only a cipher, and that the government in its search for more and more power resembles more the administrations that existed at the time of King Henry VIII or Queen Mary. In my view, Mr. Speaker, these arguments are fantastic, and the people of Canada know they are fantastic. Parliament was never more supreme than it is now, never more sovereign than it is at the present time. The government of this land is still responsible to parliament, and parliament is still responsible to the people whom each of us here represents.
A good deal has also been said during the debate about the rule of law; that this government is overriding the general rule of law. Of course nothing could be further from the truth or from the facts. This great land of ours is still under the rule of law.
I sometimes wonder whether the official opposition is so keen about the rule of law because even the Leader of the Opposition in his speech quoted a judgment of the privy council which upheld an act of this parliament. He seemed to feel that this decision of the privy council would indicate that if we in this house passed this bill the courts would probably uphold it as valid; but is that not the rule of law? That is what courts are for. There is my point, Mr. Speaker. Fortunately we still live under the rule of law. If this bill is invalid-and I do not think it is- our courts are here to declare it invalid.
Canada is a land with a constitution set up under the British North America Act, a country whose constitution is still the fundamental law of the land. Parliament is still supreme and the rule of law still exists, and every last person in this country knows it.
The Defence Production Act, as I see it-
I stand to be corrected-is to protect the public generally in a moment of crisis and at a time of emergency. The Canadian people want it and we on this side of the house want 

it, and we are going to vote for it and against the Conservative amendment.

Mr. Speaker, I have listened for a considerable length of time now to the debate on this bill. First of all I wish to compliment the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Churchill) at least on the style and spirit of his speech, but at the same time I submit that a great deal of what has been said in this debate- without in any way being critical of those who exercised their right as opposition members, since I am one of those who like to exercise that right-has been quite beside the point; because the real issue, as I see it, is not whether the government is taking away the rights of parliament.
So long as the house is called into session every year, so long as all the departments have to submit their estimates to hon. members, and so long as hon. members have the right to pass upon those estimates, there is no question about the supremacy of parliament. No department, this or any other, can function unless this house passes the appropriations necessary.
Therefore it seems to me the real question as to the need for a defence production department lies not in that department but in the Department of National Defence. So long as this house is of the opinion that we should be spending in the neighbourhood of $2 billion a year for national defence there will be no question about the necessity for a department operating under an act passed by this parliament, which should be responsible for providing the goods and services required by the Department of National Defence.
Hon. members of the Progressive Conservative party to my right have had quite a field day, and I have enjoyed listening to the speakers. Many of them have risen to great heights of oratory, and I compliment them on it, but sometimes in their eloquence they have run away with themselves. The hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre did that to a very marked degree this afternoon. At the beginning of my remarks I complimented him on his style of eloquence. I still do, but a careful reading of the content of what he said will give one more amusement than enlightenment, because he made a great deal of the fact that it was his party, the Progressive Conservative party, that was out to defend the rights, privileges and freedoms of this country, and it was the Liberal party that was out to destroy those freedoms and take away the rights of parliament, and so on.

I wish it were as clear-cut, as black and white as that. Then of course it would be a simple matter for the people of Canada to decide. If they wanted to preserve their freedoms, then of course they would have to favour the Progressive Conservative party. But as a former school teacher, the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre-and, incidentally, all the other historians in that party-should have taken the trouble to go back a little in Hansard and read some of the speeches made in this very chamber in 1935, and I have no doubt for many years before that. In that session of 1935 particularly one would have wondered, if one could hear those speeches made again without mentioning the names of those who made them, which side of the house they were coming from.
The hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre went back a great many years in discussing the fight for freedom. I will say this, that if the late Lord Bennett were able to hear that speech this afternoon he would be surprised and astonished at the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre. I say that because those were the exact words he used in this house in replying to exactly the same type of criticism which came from the same side of the house, because at that time of course Mr. Bennett was prime minister and was sitting on the other side.
I shall place on the record the exact reference. On January 21, 1935, as reported at page 32 of Hansard, Mr. King, then leader of the opposition, was criticizing some of the powers that had been granted to the government of the day, and made reference to government by order in council and various other phrases very reminiscent of what we have been hearing from our colleagues to the right in the last couple of weeks. This is the particular passage I should like to place on the record. If it were not the late Right Hon. Mackenzie King speaking one could easily attribute it to the present Leader of the Opposition. These are the words:
On occasions in the past the Prime Minister has criticized me and hon. gentlemen on this side for having taken up a considerable amount of time In the house in discussing constitutional questions. May I say that we have done so because we have looked upon the constitution of our country as the safeguard of its liberties and as the home of its freedom. When I have seen steps dismantling the constitution, gradually destroying the home of the freedom and liberties of the people, I have opposed them just as strongly as I possibly could, and I shall continue to do so no matter by what name measures of the kind may be designated.
These are words that are easy to agree with if the circumstances were being correctly described at the time; but is that not exactly what the present Leader of the Opposition
Defence Production Act and his supporters have been saying to the present government? Here is the reply of the then prime minister, the late Lord Bennett. The very next day he replied by saying, as reported at page 79 of Hansard:
When I hear the right hon. gentleman talk of the derogation of the rights of parliament I am surprised. I do not know that I am so much surprised as astonished, for it seems impossible that anyone who has been in this house as long as my right hon. friend has been, who has seen bills introduced and given first, second and third readings and passed through both houses of parliament, that conferred upon given individuals the authority and power to exercise certain functions, if the occasion should demand, should know better than to say that this is a usurpation of the powers of parliament.
I should like to draw particular attention to one phrase in that reply, where Lord Bennett stated "the power to exercise certain functions" and powers "if the occasion should demand". Is that not exactly what is being criticized today? The Bennett administration had received certain powers from parliament which they stated were not required at that time but which might have to be used under certain circumstances. It was the then leader of the opposition, the late Right Hon. Mackenzie King, who was describing that type of legislation as the dismantling of the constitution and the destroying of the liberty and freedom of the Canadian people. With that quotation on the record, and many more such quotations on the record, it is quite easy to conclude that a great deal of this battle of words has been carried on in a sort of vacuum.
The people of Canada should realize that when the Conservative administration was in power in this country and took certain powers they felt were required to meet the emergency at that time-and it was not a war emergency, incidentally, but an economic one -the Liberals then in opposition said the liberty of the Canadian people was going down the drain, the constitution was being dismantled and this was the very end.
Now the shoe is on the other foot. With the Liberals in power, the Conservatives in opposition are saying the same thing. That kind of thing is very confusing to the Canadian public and may cause new alarm and anxiety. People may actually believe that something is being done here which is an attempt to set up a dictatorship or bring about a condition where parliament will no longer have any control over the actions of the government. That simply is not the case.
The case is simply this. If the official opposition does not believe it is necessary to have a Department of Defence Production, then of course they have every right and duty to continue to oppose this bill so long as it is possible for them to do so.

If the administration uses its position at any time, not necessarily under a bill of this kind but under any authority given to it to abuse that power or to seek any special advantage for any group or individual, or does anything which in the opinion of the members of this house is not correct, then it is the duty of the members of this house, whether they sit in opposition or on the other side of the house, to protest.
That is exactly why I said a while ago that I was amazed that if the official opposition really felt that these powers contained in this bill-and I am admitting that they are very considerable powers-are as dangerous as they claim, they should have been unable to provide us with a few specific examples of where those powers have been misused or abused to the extent of causing harm to any individual or industry in this country.
On the other hand, even the members of the official opposition should be quite ready to admit that the people most closely concerned with this bill other than the government itself, that is those who take defence contracts under this act, are the ones who have not-and I emphasize this-have not raised any complaint. Nor have they expressed any fear; or if they have, it has certainly not been quoted in this house.
Under those circumstances it is stretching the situation considerably to try to frighten the Canadian public into thinking that here is something aimed at taking away the freedom of the Canadian people, because it provides the machinery or tools which will supply the Department of Defence Production with the things required for the national defence of Canada.
While we have a duty as members of the opposition to criticize-I certainly have not been backward at any time I found it necessary to criticize, and I shall not be in the future-it seems to me we have a responsibility as well. We have a responsibility not to use that position to provide purely political opposition to something because we happen to be in the opposition. We have to realize that we are going to have a defence production department, and if that department is going to do the job it is set up to do then we will have to let the administration proceed with

Then the first time we can get hold of an instance where they have abused that power or used it against the public interest, that is the time for the members of the opposition to get on their feet and raise a protest. I shall be one of those, if I am still here, to join with them. But it seems to me that a great deal of what has been said has been based purely on the idea of opposing this measure for the sake of opposing it.

That was in March of 1951, when there was a war and we had forces in the front lines. We have had no such reasons given at this time. This country is not in such a state of emergency. The powers that were in the act at that time were emergency powers, and I claim that in peacetime-I impress that point upon the house, this is peacetime-such powers are not needed permanently.
The hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Brown), who spoke a few moments ago, mentioned that in this country we were living by the rule of law. I agree with him that that is what we hope to do. I should like to give a short quotation to prove that we should protect the rule of law. It is found in the report of a special committee of the Senate which sat in 1950 and heard a lot of evidence and submissions on human rights and fundamental freedoms. Here is one paragraph from that report, which is signed by Senator A. W. Roebuck:
Canadians have individually decided that Canada shall be a land of the free. That here men shall live in the rule of law, in security of person, and that none shall oppress. Equality of right is basic


in Canadian thought and must be assured in Canadian law, so that men may live confidently in selfrespect associating freely and expressing their thoughts without fear.
That gives an idea of what parliament stands for; the rule of law does enter into it. Powers such as are contained in the Defence Production Act, if they are put on the statute books in perpetuity, do interfere with the rule of law. I have just as much right to my opinion as anyone, and I am satisfied that no court would decide otherwise. No government or department of government should have the perpetual right to the use of these powers, and that is the crux of our argument. We are not saying you should not have a department or you should not have these powers for three or four years. What we are arguing for, and we cannot seem to get it across to the government, is to have the people of this country treated the same as the British government treats the people in England.
That means that when circumstances do arise such as those which arose in this country in 1951 and the country needs special powers for the maintenance of order and the protection of its territory, those powers are given temporarily. We have no objection to a government having them, but there should be conditions attached. Parliament always has, Mr. Speaker-and I have not heard a case to the contrary-given these powers to the executive subject to certain conditions that necessitate the government making a declaration of emergency when the country is in imminent danger.
I think that is very necessary. When a declaration of emergency is made it sets before the people the facts of the situation. It alerts the people to the necessity for assisting the government to meet whatever emergency we are facing. I think that is a good thing, because it has been the history of this country that our people respond to the call of the government if there is an emergency which has been properly proclaimed.
I do not think there is any question but that industry, too, has responded. I believe the minister has stated-he will correct me if I am wrong-that he has never had to use these powers to get the work done. I am sure it would be more democratic, and a more effective way of getting co-operation from people, if a declaration were to be made if such powers were required. Three times within the memory of those of us in the House of Commons this has happened. An emergency was declared at the time of the first great war. It was also declared at the time of the second war, and also at the time of the Korean campaign.

It seems to me that to pass this measure in peacetime would be like placing a shotgun in the hands of the executive. Under this measure the minister, or anyone he wishes to delegate, can go to an industry and, with this power behind him, can compel that industry to do anything he wishes, on the threat of being closed up. I say that is interfering with a fundamental liberty. It is interfering with our right to hold and use property. Surely that is not a good principle in any measure.
Thomas Jefferson once said, "I have a right to nothing which anyone else has the right to take away from me." If this measure passes it places in the hands of the government the right to take away liberties and rights from industry. As has been pointed out, a man may be put in jail if he does not comply. Surely if this provision were to be placed permanently on the statute books it would have a discouraging effect. Keeping in mind what Thomas Jefferson said, it is clear that in this instance the government has the right to take action as set out in the act either in time of peace or in time of war.
Our liberties should be guarded jealously by parliament. We believe it is the duty of parliament to protect the great ideals of liberty and equality, and to see that at a time like this they are preserved against the assaults of opportunism, the expediency of the passing hour, the erosion of small encroachments and the scorn of those who have no patience with general principles for the protection of our fundamental freedoms and liberties.
It seems to me that our amendment asks for something that is fair and reasonable. If this were sent to a committee I should think some compromise could be worked out. If that cannot be done then the measure should be withdrawn. No one would be hurt or injured if this bill were presented early in the next session of parliament and a committee set up to define these extraordinary powers. I believe we are all agreed that the powers are extraordinary. The Prime Minister has said so; the minister has said so; members of all parties have said so. The difference of opinion seems to be that the government has dug in its heels and said, "We want it all."
We in the official opposition are considered to be the watchdogs of legislation. I can assure hon. members it is not fun to be here, but the fact remains that we have been elected to parliament to do what we believe in our opinion should be done. I would ask hon. members supporting the government this question. What would you do if you
Defence Production Act were in opposition? How would you look at the question if you viewed it from this side of the house? I am sure I can see many members in the house who would view the question from a different standpoint. One's point of view seems to be influenced by which looking-glass he looks in. I have never had the opportunity, and perhaps never will, of sitting behind a government. But it seems to me that surely there must be times when things can be viewed in two different lights.
Some of the reasons we should be protecting these fundamental rights were stated by Mr. Himel before the Senate committee which sat in 1950. Speaking about powers delegated to the executive he said:
We have all witnessed in this modern world that governments cannot always be relied upon to respect the human rights and fundamental freedoms of the person. Our history books are replete with examples which point to the moral that it is not prudent to give government almost absolute legal power over our rights and freedoms.
Along that same line I would direct the attention of hon. members to a short passage in the judgment of Mr. Justice Angers of the exchequer court where he said, in connection with the case of Bellevue v. Minister of National Revenue as reported in Exchequer Court Reports, 1948, at page 320:
There are in my judgment too many encroachments by ministers, deputy ministers and functionaries in the judicial as well as the legislative field. And if they are not curtailed the country may, in the not too remote future, be ruled by a dictatorial government.
That does not refer necessarily to the present minister or government though it may refer to them. One's conscience should be his guide. The point is that we are talking of history, the rule of law, and the right of parliament to maintain control over the executive. I was surprised to see the hon. member for Dauphin so easily taken in. I think he must know that a debate can take place on the estimates but that you cannot change the law in that way. The law will remain there, because it is written in the statute books. One may find fault with it, one may criticize it, but that does not change it. That is the point.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to make some comments on this bill. When we had this bill before us in committee I drew the attention of hon. members to the fact that it was a rather unusual case. The petitioner introduced evidence to the effect that his wife had been suffering from drug addiction. Though the respondent indicated that she was cured, Their Honours the senators apparently were not specially interested in these details in connection with the case. Consequently it was not established whether or not the respondent had been completely cured.
In view of the fact that there are some distinguished medical practitioners in the Senate chamber, I am sorry that some of them did not sit on this case. I have a great deal of confidence in the judgment of Senators Roebuck, Barbour and Golding, who heard the case, but none of them approached the evidence from the point of view of a medical doctor. Whilst Their Honours the senators recommended that the divorce be granted on the grounds of the evidence submitted before the committee, hon. members of this chamber are under no obligation to recommend that the divorce be granted on the grounds of the evidence submitted in the other chamber.
The petitioner, very early in his evidence, gave some evidence that certainly was contradictory. I submit that hon. members should read his evidence carefully. He was questioned as follows:
Is it correct that when . . . your wife's father actually arrived at your domicile, you were at that very time injecting your wife?
The answer was:
I was not.
In the previous paragraph he was being questioned and said:
I gave her somnifeni, which was injected intravenously; that is like phenobarbital. I gave her an injection, and when her father came to my room I was giving it intravenously. As I say, that is not a narcotic; that is a drug people can have without a prescription.
Private Bills-Divorce So I submit that the evidence given by the petitioner, who is a medical doctor, should be examined with a good deal of care, and we should note the fact that this medical doctor contradicted his own evidence on the same page, namely on page 17 of the evidence.
The second point I wish to develop is that the divorce was granted on the evidence given by two young girls who apparently lived in the Ferron home some four years ago. The elder of the girls was 21 when she appeared before the other place, which would make her 17 at the time this incident is alleged to have occurred. The other girl was even younger. Eileen was only 18 when she appeared in the other place, which would make her 14 when this alleged incident occurred. May I ask hon. members to listen to the evidence given by these two girls. The first one was asked:
What time did your brother arrive at the Ferron home?
The answer was:
He arrived early Saturday morning.
The other girl was asked:
Q. Do you recall or remember at what time he arrived at the Ferron's home that particular date? A. No, I didn't. It was in the afternoon.
Q. He arrived in the afternoon?
A. Yes.
Q. Do you remember in what state he was?
This is a second series of questions which I should like to draw to the attention of the chamber. One of the young girls swore that this young man arrived in the morning; the other said it was in the afternoon. The young man's sister was asked:
Is it not true that he was intoxicated when he came there?
The answer was:
No, he was not.
The other girl, who would be 14 at the time, was asked:
Do you remember in what state he was?
The answer was:
Yes, he was intoxicated.
Then she was asked later on:
Q. He was drunk?
A. Yes.
Q. Was he drunk enough to prevent him from walking steadily?
A. Yes.
Q. Was he drunk enough to have difficulty to master his language?
A. Well, yes.
Q. Do you remember at what time he left the house that day?
A. No, I don't.
I submit that hon. members should pay attention to the fact that these young girls gave conflicting evidence as to the time the brother of one was alleged to have reached the home some four years ago. In the second

Then there was some further questioning in connection with the first witness. She was asked if she had been treated by the doctor, and she replied that she had been. Their Honours the senators were a little impatient with this type of questioning, and they did not seem to know the reason for all the questioning as to whether the girl had been a patient of the doctor. Counsel for the respondent said:
Well, I will have to give testimony myself, I will have to say what I know, right away. She had a child.
The girl was asked if she had a child, and she replied very definitely. Here is the question:

A. I am still being treated for my nerves.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think this motion points up once again the serious responsibility placed upon us here in connection with the numerous bills of this nature which come before us. As a member of the legal profession I find it rather upsetting to have piles of these papers arrive on my desk almost daily and, having regard to the manifold duties confronting a member of the house, to find it almost impossible to give them the attention they should be afforded in order that a reasoned opinion may be given on the efficacy of the work that is being done. I do not think that anyone would want to detract in any way from the work of the Senate committee. It is a big job as well as one that is probably considered in the category of the thankless jobs of work which must be done here.
I have listened to the observations of the hon. member who just spoke, and it appears to me that there is considerable substance in what he said in connection with the evidence adduced in this case. I find it most difficult to reconcile the usual type of evidence that is adduced in a court of law in a proceeding of this type with the evidence which has been accepted here and which forms the basis of the bill now before us. I would think that great reluctance might have been displayed in accepting the evidence of the two young ladies referred to by the hon. member, if for no other reason than that they were at the time, I would think, in the age classification of from 13 to 15 or 16 years. That is an age when I would think in our courts considerable stress is laid on questioning to find out whether the people who have observed what has taken place actually appreciate the total circumstances surrounding the matter at issue.
In addition, here as well-as the hon. member has mentioned-there is a very unsavoury or unhappy situation having to do with narcotics and alcohol. I have noted the remarks he has made in connection with the injections 50433-361
Private Bills-Divorce which are indicated in the evidence as having been necessary to quiet the nerves of the defendant. Whether in fact there was anything behind the necessity-that is, anything that might have been contributed to by the complainant or the aggrieved party-is something which it is difficult for us in this house, looking at the evidence, to determine.
Under the circumstances I therefore think the motion of the hon. member is reasonable. It does not necessarily mean, 1 would assume, that this particular action is disposed of unfavourably for all time, but it does mean that a closer scrutiny will be given to this evidence so that all of us might be more satisfied that justice was being done in this particular instance.

Mr. Chairman, last Friday I attended my first meeting of the house committee on divorce. I should like to take a few moments to place before hon. members my impressions of the work done by that committee on that occasion in connection with the bill now before us.
It was quite a revelation to me to find that we have going on in this building a real sideshow. I can assure every hon. member that it left me absolutely cold. I am of the opinion that most of the evidence we heard in connection with this particular case was a complete fabrication, especially that given by the two investigators who had been hired by the petitioner.
So I am rising this afternoon not so much in defence of the two parties most concerned in the case as to bring to the attention of the House of Commons and the people of Canada the fact that we, their elected representatives, are spending our time and the taxpayers' money in trying to reach fair decisions by listening to long processions of sordid, detailed evidence, decisions which I do not believe we, as the elected representatives of the people, have any moral right to make.
I think it is a disgrace to have a situation where we have a committee of 50 members, elected by the people of this country and paid $10,000 a year each, and to find on one occasion more members in attendance in that 50433-36H

divorce committee than there were in the House of Commons attending to the business of the country. I think that is a disgraceful situation.
They have to listen to the evidence. I am sure all of us who listened to that evidence were just as confused after we had heard it in its entirety as before we heard any of it.
I am not going to dwell upon the evidence because it was not taken down. I would not do so, anyway, because I am not prepared, as I said at the outset, to speak in defence of the two parties concerned.
However, I do wish to say that on that occasion we had two investigators on whose evidence by and large rested the outcome of the case-two investigators who could not agree under oath as between themselves whether it was eight o'clock or eleven o'clock in the evening when they walked up to the front door of the lady's house and asked her where a certain individual lived on that street. After they had broken down the door at 2.30 in the morning by the use of a log, the three of them getting hold of it and "one, two, three", breaking down the door-in spite of all this, and in spite of the fact that the whole house was in absolute darkness, one investigator was able to tell how the woman was dressed, the colour of everything she had on, and what she did not have on. Then one of these paid investigators said, "The woman walked out of the bedroom alone", while the other said she walked out of a different bedroom, pushing another man.
So here we had the evidence of the two key witnesses in the case. And who are these key witnesses? Who are these two supersnoops? They are the very same gentlemen to whom reference was made this afternoon in a case we have just disposed of. They are the very same gentlemen, Mr. Chairman, we heard about in this chamber last Friday. They are the same pair of peeping Toms whom we have heard about as being connected with an organization known as Reliable Detective Agency, the same gentlemen who have had unprecedented success in the 90 cases they have investigated over the last year. They are the same pair who last year in a court of justice were convicted of fabricating evidence with intent to mislead a court of justice in this country.
These were the two men, these were the two key witnesses, in a case heard before a select committee of this House of Commons. I was amazed. What amazed me most of all was the insulting and insolent manner displayed by one investigator, Pichette, who apparently, in view of his successes in this field, might very well use the slogan that

Private Bills-Divorce
he always gets his woman. This man, in a most insolent manner, stood up in the committee and challenged the attorney for the respondent, marvelling at the audacity of anyone who would question his credibility as a witness just because he had been convicted of fabricating evidence to mislead a court of justice.
These are the kind of people we are dealing with. Could not all of us in that committee hear the expression of hurt in his voice when he said that he had won his appeal? But, Mr. Chairman, he had won that appeal on the flimsy, legal technicality that a committee of the other place or a committee of the House of Commons is not a court of justice.
I say this is a ridiculous situation, and I am glad we are going to face up to it in the House of Commons. How can we deal with evidence submitted by people of this kind, people who have no sense of responsibility for what they say before a committee? I am not advocating divorce reform or anything of the kind, but I am advocating that these cases should be heard before a proper court, where investigators of the kind about which I have spoken will be made to accept some responsibility for what they say when they give evidence.
It is not my intention to say anything further at this time. I wish only to draw the attention of the committee to the absolutely ridiculous situation in which we as members of the House of Commons are placed every time we have to act on that committee.

One of the investigators told us that on one occasion he ran out of film. subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when I left off at five o'clock I was discussing why it seemed to me these extraordinary powers included in the bill should not be made part of the permanent law of the land. I have only a few minutes left, and I shall try to summarize the facts in a few words, if I may.
When the act was first passed in 1951, we were at war. We had troops in combat service. The government was faced with a situation where it had to get supplies and, as I said this afternoon, speed was of prime importance. The government had to meet their obligations abroad, and they had to meet them at home. At that time they needed extraordinary powers. Nevertheless,
Defence Production Act I should like to draw this one point to the attention of hon. members of this house to show that at that time the government and the Prime Minister must have recognized how carefully parliament regards legislation which hands over great powers to the executive, the cabinet.
Because of that realization, I believe, especially on the part of the Prime Minister, he was very careful at that time to have a time limit written into the bill. All the statements made since then, right up to now, giving them the fairest possible construction, I would summarize in this way without giving any quotations from Hansard. The most we can say about the Prime Minister's statement and the statement of the right hon. Minister of Defence Production is that they did not guess quite right about the time. They asked for the powers until 1956, but now they say they made a mistake in the time which they had guessed. In other words, the fairest construction I can put on it is that they have made out a case to ask for an extension, but they have not made out a case for asking that these extraordinary powers be written into the law in perpetuity and become part of the permanent law of this land.
There is a big difference between the government's conception of this legislation and our conception. That is why we are here. We are fighting for a principle: Will parliament become the servant of the cabinet, the executive, or will parliament remain supreme and retain these controls that history teaches us we should not allow to disappear piecemeal?
I shall just take time for a short quotation from page 317 of the evidence before the special committee of the Senate on human rights and fundamental freedoms in 1950. This was in the brief submitted by Professor Lower of Queen's University. I think it is very apt, and is something I commend to hon. members of this house to think about, because it deals with the principle of the supremacy of parliament. This is one quotation from his brief:
All I could add here would be an exhortation to members of parliament to remember the great traditions that lie behind parliament and to cultivate the independence of character and of decision which their predecessors over the last seven centuries at various critical stages of the history of the English-speaking world have shown.
I close my remarks by again asking in all fairness that further consideration be given to this bill, by adopting our amendment or by withdrawing this bill and presenting either two bills or one bill in two parts that would meet the wishes of all concerned and give the minister all he wants for a limited period. At the end of that period the matter could

Defence Production Act be reviewed, and I am certain if he came back and showed cause, as we say in court, he would have his powers renewed for another limited period.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, since this debate has commenced we have been almost inundated by a tremendous torrent of ineffectual hogwash from the hon. gentlemen in the Conservative party. To turn a Churchillian phrase, never has so much bilge been spoken for so long by so few.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext: Small laughter.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARY OF MINISTER AND EXPIRY OF ACT
speechtext:
They have talked about everything but the merits of the bill. To me at least there seems to have been a rising crescendo of personal abuse and vilification heaped upon the head of the Minister of Defence Production. By such tactics the Conservative party is fast becoming as dead as a dodo. The fact that they have resorted to such a shameful filibuster against this bill is a reflection of their political bankruptcy.
We have heard well reasoned and dispassionate accounts from the Minister of Defence Production and the Prime Minister, explanations which I am sure the Canadian people will find reasonable and which will make good common sense. The reason we have this bill before the house at the present time is because, to use Sir John A. Macdonald's expression, we are passing through troublous times. This should be fundamental to our thinking. We must divest ourselves of every other consideration for the time being. The times are extraordinary; they are dangerous. That is, for example, the reason for NATO. Because of this factor we need such a bill with teeth in it, in the national interest.
The interesting thing which the opposition has not mentioned is that in the United States and United Kingdom there are comparable statutes on the books which give those governments much more sweeping powers. We have been, and still are spending about $2 billion a year on national defence, or about 50 cents out of every dollar of taxes. Our allies, I am informed, are spending about $200 billion per year for similar purposes.
I hope this point will not be lost on hon. members opposite. We have an irrevocable obligation to meet the needs of defence in order to protect our way of life. Even through all this continuing emergency this government has produced a bill which provides adequate safeguards for the supremacy of parliament and the rule of law.
The purpose of the bill is to enable the Minister of Defence Production to make purchases for defence and to be sure that these

goods are produced in a never-ending stream. This is something I believe even hon. gentlemen opposite will concede makes good common sense. It will also give permanency to the department, an idea to which the hon. gentlemen opposite at least give lip service.
What are the safeguards to which I allude? First, the bill sets out specifically how defence production and purchasing are to be carried out. There is nothing hidden here. It is set out very clearly and very carefully in the act, with particular reference to how the freedom of the individual is safeguarded. True, property rights in an emergency can be impinged upon, a situation which is just as it should be. Let us not forget that the public interest is paramount to any-and I repeat "any"-private commercial interest, though of course my Conservative friends might disagree with me here.
As regards private individual interests and the freedom of the individual, adequate safeguards are maintained, as the minister has pointed out. The individual has access to the courts of the land if there is disagreement with regard to the prices of items. For hon. gentlemen opposite to say this is socialism is, I respectfully submit, sheer nonsense. Men who talk like that have a political and social philosophy which belongs to those gentlemen who had to be dragged, kicking and screaming, into the twentieth century, to use Mr. Adlai Stevenson's phrase.
The second safeguard to which I referred is the fact that this bill can be debated at any time the estimates of this department come up for consideration. I think perhaps my hon. friends have forgotten this extremely important aspect.
As a humble backbencher and supporter of the government, may I say that these safeguards certainly satisfy me. But the government has leaned over backward and has gone much further in order to ensure full debate on this measure. The Minister of Defence Production has painstakingly endeavoured to meet the objections of the opposition. On June 13, as reported at page 4683 of Hansard, on the orders of the day, he promised that orders made under this act, either by the minister or by the governor in council, shall be tabled at the earliest possible moment and that a notice of motion signed by ten members praying for the repeal or amendment of any such order, if brought forward within seven days of the tabling of the order, shall be debated at the first possible opportunity within the next four sitting days.
Then again just yesterday, Monday, July 4, the Prime Minister, as reported at page 5642

of Hansard, stated that at the end of three years any private member could bring in a bill to amend the Defence Production Act, that the government would treat this private bill as government business, and that it would be debatable on second reading as if it were government business. Surely, Mr. Speaker, this is going more than half-way.
What was the attitude of the historic Conservative party? This offer was brusquely and callously spurned by the Conservative party. Both the Minister of Defence Production and the Prime Minister have given, in my opinion, cogent reasons why a time limit cannot be put on this bill. The Minister of Defence Production gave us a lucid account of the terrifying responsibilities weighing on his shoulders as a result of the intensified supersonic aircraft and guided missile program.

This amendment, I say, is very appropriate, to my mind, and I do not see why it should not be unanimously accepted by this house.
May I be permitted to read the amendment over again, so as to point out to all hon. members of the house its wisdom and relevancy. This is the amendment:
That Bill No. 256, an act to amend the Defence Production Act, be not now read a second time, but that the subject matter thereof be referred to the standing committee on banking and commerce with instructions that they have power to examine and report upon the advisability of
(a)	placing the Department of Defence Production on a permanent basis and conferring on the department such powers as ought to be of a continuing nature; and
(b)	conferring for a period of one year, or until extended by parliament, such additional powers as may be strictly necessary in the light of the existing world conditions.
It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that this amendment is a most reasonable one. Anyhow, most important bills discussed in parliament during the various sessions, and particularly when they are of a somewhat contentious nature, are generally referred to some committee of the house for further study.
I think that the bill now before us may, to say the least, well be termed contentious. It may be said, I think, and rightly so, that at this stage of the session, several bills have been referred to the committees of the house. Among others, to mention but a few cases, at the very outset of the session we referred to the committee on external affairs an act respecting the construction, operation and maintenance of international river improvements (the boundary waters act). It was studied in committee, where we heard most

provincial attorneys general and all those who had representations to make about it, and I must say it came back to the house with several amendments.
Then there was an act to amend the Unemployment Insurance Act; it was studied in committee and sent back to the house with many amendments. The act to amend the Transport Act and the act to amend the Canadian National Railways Act, which consolidated into one statute the national railways legislation which was considerably amended in committee, were then submitted to the house for adoption. Many other measures were referred to the appropriate committees of the house and, after a more thorough examination, after all the representations made by various provincial governments or public bodies were received, the measures were sent back to the house with amendments which definitely made them better every time.
Here is a measure which we are asked to consider, certainly one of the most important the house has had to study for many years, this being the opinion of the press in general and of everyone interested in Canadian politics. I do not see why such an important measure should not be also referred to the committee as requested by the member for Royal in his amendment.
This bill, designed to amend chapter 62 of the Revised Statutes of Canada, by dropping section 41, has far-reaching implications since it would put all the other sections on a permanent basis. If one reads these sections, it is very hard to convince oneself that the Minister of Defence Production really needs all those extraordinary powers to ensure the defence of our country in peacetime.

Mr. Speaker, there is only one reason why this debate should continue. That reason is the insistence of the government on proceeding with an act which is entirely unnecessary, which is contrary to the clear undertaking given to this house in 1951, and which should not, in any event, have been presented to us at this time.
Many hon. members had been waiting to hear the statement of the Prime Minister in regard to this measure. We heard from him yesterday. In that speech he repeated, almost in exact terms, the statement made by the Minister of Defence Production. His words are to be found at page 5643 of Hansard:

we are not prepared to put any definite time limit upon it at this time.
That is the reason we are here. There has been some tendency to call this a filibuster. Any hon. member can call it what he likes.

The fact is that we are exercising our democratic right and our democratic duty to place before this parliament reasons why the government should not go back on its own statement made in 1951. It was this government -this same government that now asks us to remove any time limit-which told us there were in this act powers which should not be continued.
Today we are asked to make them permanent. Do not let any hon. member opposite say that the word "permanent" goes too far. That was the word used by the Minister of Defence Production. He used the word "permanent". The intention of this amending bill of two sections is to make permanent, as part of the law of our land, provisions which by-pass parliament.
I think there must be disappointment in the mind of every hon. member that the Prime Minister, as head of the government, as a lawyer, and as the honorary president of the Canadian Bar Association, did not tell us something of his own concept of the supremacy of parliament and the rule of law. There were times when he did not shun discussion of this subject. There were times when he did not think this was something to be passed over and ignored. There were times when he thought this was perhaps the most important thing that could engage the temporal discussion of any Canadian citizen. Why have we not heard from him as to what this act does mean? Why have we not heard from him some correction of the misstatements of the Minister of Defence Production with regard to the effect of this act?
The Minister of Defence Production has told us that the powers of this act are narrower than those of the corresponding acts in the United Kingdom and the United States. The Prime Minister knows that is not so. The Prime Minister could well have made a comparison of these acts.
Let us concede that the Minister of Defence Production, who asserts that he was responsible for the draftsmanship of this act, was unaware of its consequences. The Prime Minister is not unaware of them. The Prime Minister is not unaware that there are subjects at issue here that go far beyond the question of confidence in the minister. We were perfectly frank in stating why we were continuing this debate. We are perfectly frank now in saying why we continue this debate.
We know that unless there is a revival of conscience and responsibility on the part of the Liberal members of the house, ultimately the act will pass. We hope, however, that it will not pass, because we still hope that a free press will assert itself and that the
Defence Production Act
members will not be unconscious of the fact that right across Canada today editors of responsible newspapers are expressing opinions which are strongly opposed to the indefinite continuance of these powers without any refinement or redrafting.
The suggestion was made, Mr. Speaker, that we had suddenly, at this stage, started opposing this measure simply for the sake of opposition. For that reason it becomes necessary to remind hon. members opposite of exactly what did take place. This act did not come before us just within the past few weeks. On March 10, almost four months ago, after notice had been on the order paper for some time, a motion was presented to the house by the Prime Minister asking the house to declare that it was expedient that a bill be introduced to amend the Defence Production Act.
At that time there was a discussion of this subject. As has already been pointed out, it was then suggested that appropriate steps be taken to give permanence to the Department of Defence Production and to remove from the act those arbitrary powers which the government itself had said should not be continued.
Since it has been suggested that we have merely been conducting factious opposition at this stage, I wish to quote briefly from what I said at that time, when this motion was under discussion. I quote from page 1985 of Hansard for March 14 of this year:
We all recognize the need for a Department of Defence Production. We all recognize that this department should have the necessary authority to acquire the necessary materials which are essential and to direct the production of those things which can be used in our participation in the joint defence of freedom.
I then went on to point out the position the government had taken when this measure was before us in 1951, and later in the debate I had this to say as recorded at page 1987:
. . . the nature of the threat of any departure from long established practices is not to be measured by what has happened: it should be measured by what could happen at some other time. I am not attributing to any member of the government any motives other than those stated by those who have put forward their support of this measure. In these serious days we are all citizens of Canada deeply concerned about the future of Canadians growing up in this great land of ours and their freedom in the years ahead. I would not seek to draw any distinction between the sentiments of any member in this house in regard to the future of Canada, and of the people who will live in it in the years ahead. The statement has been repeated to us over and over again that this may be a long and tedious struggle for freedom, which we hope will reach a secure peace in the years ahead without the blight of such a terrible war as is now pictured to us as a possibility.
Let us break new ground. Even though four years ago it may have seemed wise in the mind
